Individual mones can differentiate phenotypes (e.g., tumor vs normal) with statistical significance.
Mones form clusters with strong correlations that are preserved across related cancer types.
Linear models based on mones can accurately classify tumors and cancer types (high AUC).
Mones have interpretable correlations with gene expression, e.g., collagen genes in ovarian cancer and immune genes in colon and lung cancers.
Mone analysis provides interpretability without requiring a trained classifier.
papers.limitation:
Correlation does not imply causation.
Some mones' ability to distinguish tumor from normal is impacted by differences between frozen and FFPE modalities.
future_direction: Investigate the utility of mones for other image analysis tasks, such as survival prediction and virtual staining.
Integrate mones with other data modalities, such as genomic and clinical data, to enhance interpretability and predictive power.

papers.title: Sparse autoencoders reveal selective remapping of visual concepts during adaptation
papers.research_question: How do prompt-based adaptation techniques change the association of model inputs to interpretable concepts in CLIP, and does adaptation activate new concepts or reuse existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PatchSAE, a sparse autoencoder for vision transformers that provides spatial attribution of interpretable concepts, and finds that prompt-based adaptation improves performance primarily by adding new mappings between existing concepts and downstream classes, rather than activating new concepts.
papers.conclusion: PatchSAE is an effective tool for interpreting vision transformers, and prompt-based adaptation methods like MaPLe work by remapping existing visual concepts to new class labels rather than learning fundamentally new concepts.
papers.key_findings:
PatchSAE identifies diverse interpretable concepts (from simple visual patterns to high-level semantics) and provides spatial attribution of these concepts in images.
SAE latents contain class discriminative information, as ablating top-activating latents per class significantly reduces classification accuracy.
Prompt-based adaptation (MaPLe) and the original CLIP model activate a highly overlapping set of SAE latents, indicating similar concepts are recognized.
The performance gain from adaptation stems from tailoring the mapping between commonly activated concepts and downstream task classes, not from firing additional class-discriminative concepts.
PatchSAE trained on CLIP generalizes to the adapted model MaPLe, allowing comparison in a shared latent space.
papers.limitation: The scope of this work focuses on the CLIP vision encoder. Analysis of different vision encoders and joint analysis of multimodality could provide more comprehensive understanding.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to different vision encoders.
Jointly analyzing the multimodality of vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Adapting foundation models for specific purposes has become a standard approach to build machine learning systems for downstream applications. Yet, it is an open question which mechanisms take place during adaptation. Here we develop a new Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) for the CLIP vision transformer, named PatchSAE, to extract interpretable concepts at granular levels (e.g., shape, color, or semantics of an object) and their patch-wise spatial attributions. We explore how these concepts influence the model output in downstream image classification tasks and investigate how recent state-of-the-art prompt-based adaptation techniques change the association of model inputs to these concepts. While activations of concepts slightly change between adapted and non-adapted models, we find that the majority of gains on common adaptation tasks can be explained with the existing concepts already present in the non-adapted foundation model. This work provides a concrete framework to train and use SAEs for Vision Transformers and provides insights into explaining adaptation mechanisms.

papers.title: Transformer-Based Explainable Deep Learning for Breast Cancer Detection in Mammography: The MammoFormer Framework
papers.research_question: How can transformer-based models be effectively integrated with feature enhancement and explainable AI to improve breast cancer detection in mammography and overcome clinical adoption barriers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the MammoFormer framework, which integrates transformer architectures with feature enhancement and explainable AI to improve breast cancer detection accuracy and interpretability for clinical adoption.
papers.conclusion: The MammoFormer framework successfully integrates transformers, feature enhancement, and explainable AI to achieve high accuracy and clinical interpretability for breast cancer detection, providing a blueprint for AI-driven diagnostic tools.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer models with feature enhancement (especially HOG) achieve performance comparable to CNNs, with ViT reaching 99.0% accuracy.
HOG features provide the most reliable enhancement, yielding an average accuracy of 98.4% across models.
Multiple XAI techniques (Integrated Gradients, GradCAM, Occlusion, etc.) consistently highlight clinically relevant regions, enhancing interpretability.
The ResNet-50 model with original images achieves 99.9% accuracy, making it suitable for primary screening.
The MammoFormer framework's tiered deployment strategy allows seamless integration into clinical workflows, from routine screening to complex case analysis.
future_direction: Clinical validation of the MammoFormer framework.
Exploration of hybrid approaches combining CNN robustness with transformer global modeling.
Extension to other medical imaging modalities and testing on diverse datasets.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer detection through mammography interpretation remains difficult because of the minimal nature of abnormalities that experts need to identify alongside the variable interpretations between readers. The potential of CNNs for medical image analysis faces two limitations: they fail to process both local information and wide contextual data adequately and do not provide explainable AI (XAI) operations which doctors need to accept them in clinics. The researcher developed the MammoFormer framework which unites transformer-based architecture with multi-feature enhancement components and XAI functionalities within one framework. Seven different architectures consisting of CNNs, Vision Transformer, Swin Transformer, and ConvNext were tested alongside four enhancement techniques, including original images, negative transformation, adaptive histogram equalization, and histogram of oriented gradients. The MammoFormer framework addresses critical clinical adoption barriers of AI mammography systems through: (1) systematic optimization of transformer architectures via architecture-specific feature enhancement, achieving up to 13% performance improvement, (2) comprehensive explainable AI integration providing multi-perspective diagnostic interpretability, and (3) a clinically deployable ensemble system combining CNN reliability with transformer global context modeling. The combination of transformer models with suitable feature enhancements enables them to achieve equal or better results than CNN approaches. ViT achieves 98.3% accuracy alongside AHE while Swin Transformer gains a 13.0% advantage through HOG enhancements. Five XAI techniques, including Integrated Gradients, GradCAM, Occlusion, DeepLIFT and Saliency maps demonstrate that transformer models effectively recognize diagnostically significant features by capturing long-range dependencies in mammograms. Using HOG features provides the most reliable enhancement impact (98.4% average accuracy) among all visualization methods. MammoFormer establishes a clinical breast cancer screening workflow with diagnostic precision and interpretability through its simultaneous implementation of architectural design with feature enhancement and explainability features.

papers.title: Learning Brain Tumor Representation in 3D High-Resolution MR Images via Interpretable State Space Models
papers.research_question: How to design an efficient and interpretable model for 3D high-resolution MR images that overcomes the computational and interpretability limitations of Vision Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: We propose a linearly scaled SSM-based masked autoencoder for 3D high-resolution MR images that achieves state-of-the-art performance on glioma classification tasks and provides interpretability through a novel latent-to-spatial mapping technique.
papers.conclusion: The proposed SSM-based model efficiently processes high-resolution 3D MR images, achieves state-of-the-art performance on glioma classification, and provides interpretable representations via latent-to-spatial mapping, demonstrating potential for radiomics analysis and clinical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The SSM-based model outperforms Vanilla ViT and 3D ResNet baselines on IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion classification tasks.
The model scales linearly with sequence length, enabling the use of smaller patch sizes (e.g., 4) and capturing fine-grained details, leading to improved performance.
The latent-to-spatial mapping provides interpretable saliency maps that highlight tumor regions, offering insights into the model's decision-making process.
The model is robust to rotations but sensitive to severe bias field distortions, indicating the importance of careful data pre-processing.
Masked image modeling pre-training yields more balanced performance across tasks compared to contrastive learning and no pre-training.
papers.limitation:
The unpatchify algorithm for latent-to-spatial mapping may lose finer spatial details due to information compression during patchification, limiting precise spatial correspondence.
The model's generalizability to different pre-processing variations and unseen data needs improvement.
future_direction: Refine the unpatchify process or develop alternative strategies to better preserve anatomical details during reconstruction.
Improve model generalizability to different pre-processing variations and unseen data.
Train on larger and more diverse medical imaging datasets to enhance applicability to downstream tasks like segmentation and detection.
papers.abstract: Learning meaningful and interpretable representations from high-dimensional volumetric magnetic resonance (MR) images is essential for advancing personalized medicine. While Vision Transformers (ViTs) have shown promise in handling image data, their application to 3D multi-contrast MR images faces challenges due to computational complexity and interpretability. To address this, we propose a novel state-space-model (SSM)-based masked autoencoder which scales ViT-like models to handle high-resolution data effectively while also enhancing the interpretability of learned representations. We propose a latent-to-spatial mapping technique that enables direct visualization of how latent features correspond to specific regions in the input volumes in the context of SSM. We validate our method on two key neuro-oncology tasks: identification of isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation status and 1p/19q co-deletion classification, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy. Our results highlight the potential of SSM-based self-supervised learning to transform radiomics analysis by combining efficiency and interpretability.

papers.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Medical Imaging: Techniques, Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques be applied in medical imaging to enhance interpretability, transparency, and clinical trust?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques in medical imaging, discussing their applications, challenges, and future directions to enhance interpretability and clinical trust.
papers.conclusion: XAI is crucial for bridging the gap between high-performing deep learning models and the need for interpretability in clinical environments, with future work needed to address challenges and improve usability.
papers.key_findings:
Feature visualization techniques like Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients are widely used to highlight important image regions in medical diagnostics.
Attention mechanisms improve model interpretability by focusing on relevant regions, but lack standardized metrics for clinical validation.
Rule-based and symbolic XAI approaches offer high interpretability and align well with clinical guidelines, as demonstrated in vertebral fracture detection.
Example-based methods, such as case-based reasoning, provide intuitive explanations by referencing similar past cases, enhancing clinical trust.
Major challenges include the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability, ethical concerns, and integration barriers in clinical workflows.
future_direction: Refining example-based techniques for better interpretability.
Developing ethical frameworks to address bias and privacy concerns.
Improving generalizability and performance of explainable models.
papers.abstract: The integration of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) into medical imaging is pivotal in addressing the “black-box” limitations of deep learning models, which often hinder clinical trust and regulatory approval. This review provides a comprehensive examination of XAI techniques that enhance interpretability and transparency in diagnostic imaging applications. Key approaches such as feature visualization (Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients), attention mechanisms, symbolic reasoning, and example-based methods—are explored alongside their practical implementations. Specific cases in cardiac imaging, cancer diagnostics, and brain lesion segmentation illustrate the value of XAI in improving clinical decision-making and patient care. Moreover, the review highlights major challenges, including the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability, ethical and legal constraints, integration barriers within clinical workflows, and the complexity of medical data. To address these issues, future research directions are proposed, including the development of more robust example-based models, ethical frameworks, generalizable architectures, advanced visualization techniques, and interdisciplinary collaboration. With continued refinement and responsible deployment, XAI systems can enable AI models to become not only accurate but also interpretable and clinically relevant. This paper underscores the transformative potential of XAI in building trustworthy, transparent, and effective AI-driven diagnostic tools aligned with the practical demands of modern healthcare systems.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Vision Transformer Visualization: What Neurons Tell and How Neurons Behave?
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers (ViTs) behave and what are their intriguing properties, such as robustness to image occlusions and patch shuffling?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a visualization technique to expose the information carried in neurons and embeddings across ViT layers, revealing that ViTs are robust to occlusions and patch shuffling, and that embeddings exhibit clustering behavior by object type at higher layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a visualization technique for ViTs, leading to findings including the clustering behavior of embeddings, which is explained mathematically and verified experimentally.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs are robust to image occlusions and patch shuffling, as visualized by the proposed technique.
Level 0 embeddings already carry rich semantic details, unlike CNNs where low-level filters capture only edges or lines.
Filters at layer 0 are powerful and can activate multiple object types across images.
Feature embeddings across layers show clustering behavior, becoming more separated by object type at higher layers, with higher attention weights for object patches.
A mathematical explanation is provided for the clustering behavior, and it is quantitatively verified on the Pascal VOC dataset.
papers.limitation: The clustering behavior of feature embeddings has not been exploited in real-world applications.
future_direction: Exploit the clustering behavior using contrastive learning to create more contrastive feature embeddings for downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Recently vision transformers (ViT) have been applied successfully for various tasks in computer vision. However, important questions such as why they work or how they behave still remain largely unknown. In this paper, we propose an effective visualization technique, to assist us in exposing the information carried in neurons and feature embeddings across the ViT's layers. Our approach departs from the computational process of ViTs with a focus on visualizing the local and global information in input images and the latent feature embeddings at multiple levels. Visualizations at the input and embeddings at level 0 reveal interesting findings such as providing support as to why ViTs are rather generally robust to image occlusions and patch shuffling; or unlike CNNs, level 0 embeddings already carry rich semantic details. Next, we develop a rigorous framework to perform effective visualizations across layers, exposing the effects of ViTs filters and grouping/clustering behaviors to object patches. Finally, we provide comprehensive experiments on real datasets to qualitatively and quantitatively demonstrate the merit of our proposed methods as well as our findings. https://github.com/byM1902/ViT_visualization

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: On Interpretability of Deep Learning based Skin Lesion Classifiers using Concept Activation Vectors
papers.research_question: Does a deep learning based skin lesion classifier learn and utilize human-understandable disease-related concepts similar to those used by dermatologists?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel training and significance testing paradigm for Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) and demonstrates that a skin lesion classifier learns and uses human-understandable disease-related concepts similar to those used by dermatologists.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that deep learning based skin lesion classifiers learn and use human-understandable concepts similar to those used by dermatologists, increasing confidence in such CAD systems. The proposed method using identically distributed images for CAV training is effective.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers trained on network activations achieve significantly higher validation accuracies than random baseline, indicating that the latent space encodes human-understandable concepts.
TCAV scores show that disease-related concepts influence predictions in a way consistent with medical knowledge: benign concepts positively affect Naevi class and negatively affect Melanoma, while malignant concepts do the opposite.
The model's use of concepts aligns with dermatological criteria, e.g., atypical pigment network, irregular streaks, regression structures, etc., are positively associated with Melanoma.
The method can sort test images by concept visibility, providing per-image explanations.
The novel training paradigm using identically distributed data for CAV training is effective for skin lesion classification.
papers.limitation: Subjective annotations by experts and small number of concept training samples limit thorough analysis of all concepts.
future_direction: Curating high-quality datasets with reliable fine-grained concept labels.
Extending the approach to unsupervised concept discovery to eliminate the need for expert annotations.
papers.abstract: Deep learning based medical image classifiers have shown remarkable prowess in various application areas like ophthalmology, dermatology, pathology, and radiology. However, the acceptance of these Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems in real clinical setups is severely limited primarily because their decision-making process remains largely obscure. This work aims at elucidating a deep learning based medical image classifier by verifying that the model learns and utilizes similar disease-related concepts as described and employed by dermatologists. We used a well-trained and high performing neural network developed by REasoning for COmplex Data (RECOD) Lab for classification of three skin tumours, i.e. Melanocytic Naevi, Melanoma and Seborrheic Keratosis and performed a detailed analysis on its latent space. Two well established and publicly available skin disease datasets, PH <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and derm7pt, are used for experimentation. Human understandable concepts are mapped to RECOD image classification model with the help of Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), introducing a novel training and significance testing paradigm for CAVs. Our results on an independent evaluation set clearly shows that the classifier learns and encodes human understandable concepts in its latent representation. Additionally, TCAV scores (Testing with CAVs) suggest that the neural network indeed makes use of disease-related concepts in the correct way when making predictions. We anticipate that this work can not only increase confidence of medical practitioners on CAD but also serve as a stepping stone for further development of CAV-based neural network interpretation methods.

papers.title: Explaining Explainability: Recommendations for Effective Use of Concept Activation Vectors
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three properties of Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs): inconsistency across layers, entanglement with other concepts, and spatial dependency, and how they affect model explanations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates three properties of Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) that affect interpretability, introduces tools to detect these properties, and provides recommendations for effective use of CAVs.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that CAVs have three key properties (inconsistency, entanglement, spatial dependence) that can lead to misleading explanations, and provides recommendations to mitigate these issues.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs are not consistent across layers, which can lead to contradictory TCAV scores and misleading explanations.
CAVs can be entangled with other concepts, meaning they represent multiple concepts simultaneously, leading to uninterpretable explanations.
CAVs can be spatially dependent, encoding location-specific information, which affects their interpretation.
The choice of negative probe set can have a substantial impact on the meaning of a CAV.
Understanding these properties can be used to advantage, e.g., using spatially dependent CAVs to test translation invariance in CNNs.
future_direction: Investigating alternative forms of representation, such as clusters within activation space, and assessing their relative merits.
papers.abstract: Concept-based explanations translate the internal representations of deep learning models into a language that humans are familiar with: concepts. One popular method for finding concepts is Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which are learnt using a probe dataset of concept exemplars. In this work, we investigate three properties of CAVs: (1) inconsistency across layers, (2) entanglement with other concepts, and (3) spatial dependency. Each property provides both challenges and opportunities in interpreting models. We introduce tools designed to detect the presence of these properties, provide insight into how each property can lead to misleading explanations, and provide recommendations to mitigate their impact. To demonstrate practical applications, we apply our recommendations to a melanoma classification task, showing how entanglement can lead to uninterpretable results and that the choice of negative probe set can have a substantial impact on the meaning of a CAV. Further, we show that understanding these properties can be used to our advantage. For example, we introduce spatially dependent CAVs to test if a model is translation invariant with respect to a specific concept and class. Our experiments are performed on natural images (ImageNet), skin lesions (ISIC 2019), and a new synthetic dataset, Elements. Elements is designed to capture a known ground truth relationship between concepts and classes. We release this dataset to facilitate further research in understanding and evaluating interpretability methods.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: An interpretable graph neural network for histological image analysis
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interpretable Graph Neural Network for histological image analysis that overcomes limitations of traditional message-passing architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel interpretable Graph Neural Network based on activation maps and Self-Organizing Maps for histological image analysis, which models neighborhood representation while maintaining interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to histopathological image analysis by proposing novel research tools, annotated data, and an interpretable GNN method, paving the way for more accurate and reliable AI-based personalized medicine.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed activation map-based GNN achieves competitive performance on citation network benchmarks.
The method provides interpretable activation maps that reveal tissue microenvironments in histological images.
Using an overlap between 1/2 and 2/3 when extracting tiles from whole slide images improves model accuracy.
The dataset construction workflow enabled by the WSI2ML software effectively improves annotation quality over iterations.
future_direction: Improving the annotation software with additional features.
Expanding the neoadjuvant gastric histological tissue dataset.
Extending the activation map-based GNN to other domains and architectures.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancements in machine learning have opened up new possibilities for solving complex problems, including in highly specialized applications with notable impact on relevant diseases, such as cancer. A critical aspect of cancer treatment is histopathological image analysis, a field that analyzes large zoomable images at a microscope level, to understand how the disease affected the patient, enabling patient-tailored treatment strategies. However, progress in this area relies heavily on interdisciplinary collaboration and the development of methods that utilize highquality annotated datasets effectively. In this thesis, we address these challenges by proposing a new collaborative annotation software for Whole Slides Images. Using the software, we aid in the construction of novel annotated datasets with application-specific goals. Then, inspired by the pathologist\'s work methodology, we develop a novel Graph Neural Network (GNN) technique based on activation maps that models neighborhood representation based on the presence or absence of features in the neighborhood. Our approach is based on the Message Passing architecture, which although very popular, may limit graph representation by suffering from issues such as limited injectability and oversquashing, depending on the GNN architecture and task. Moreover, increasing traditional GNN\'s receptive field requires deepening the neural network, which introduces additional challenges, such as higher computational requirements. In contrast, our approach projects the graph\'s features to a fixed-size map representation with Self-Organizing Maps, which are activated based on the presence and distance of features from the central node, within the model\'s configurable receptive field. Lastly, the activation map keeps the graph\'s features within their original domain during aggregation, which has benefits for interpretability. We conclude this work by training the proposed GNN on a novel annotated dataset developed with the proposed tool, and using its interpretability advantages to highlight the patterns it identifies, contrasting it with a pathologist\'s expectations. This work contributes to the advancement of histopathological image analysis by proposing novel research tools, annotated data, and methods, paving the way for more accurate and reliable AI-based personalized medicine.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Identifying Interpretable Subspaces in Image Representations
papers.research_question: How can we automatically explain features in image representations using natural language concepts? Also, which features in the representation space are explainable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces FALCON, an automatic framework for explaining image representation features using natural language concepts. It also shows that interpretable subspaces are often composed of feature groups rather than individual features.
papers.conclusion: FALCON provides an effective way to automatically explain features in image representations. The study reveals that interpretable subspaces often consist of feature groups, and the extracted concepts can be used for debugging and transfer.
papers.key_findings:
FALCON can automatically extract human-understandable concepts for features without human intervention.
Individual features are often not interpretable, but groups of features are more interpretable.
FALCON concepts are validated by human evaluation with high precision and recall.
Concepts can be used to explain failures in downstream tasks.
Concepts can be transferred across representation spaces via a linear transformation.
papers.limitation:
The quality of explanations is dependent on the captioning dataset and the vision-language model.
The method may not capture very high-level abstract concepts that are not well-represented in the captioning data.
future_direction: Extending FALCON to other modalities like text and audio.
Improving the concept extraction to handle more abstract features.
Exploring the use of FALCON for model editing and improving model robustness.
papers.abstract: We propose Automatic Feature Explanation using Contrasting Concepts (FALCON), an interpretability framework to explain features of image representations. For a target feature, FALCON captions its highly activating cropped images using a large captioning dataset (like LAION-400m) and a pre-trained vision-language model like CLIP. Each word among the captions is scored and ranked leading to a small number of shared, human-understandable concepts that closely describe the target feature. FALCON also applies contrastive interpretation using lowly activating (counterfactual) images, to eliminate spurious concepts. Although many existing approaches interpret features independently, we observe in state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised models, that less than 20% of the representation space can be explained by individual features. We show that features in larger spaces become more interpretable when studied in groups and can be explained with high-order scoring concepts through FALCON. We discuss how extracted concepts can be used to explain and debug failures in downstream tasks. Finally, we present a technique to transfer concepts from one (explainable) representation space to another unseen representation space by learning a simple linear transformation. Code available at https://github.com/NehaKalibhat/falcon-explain.

papers.title: Rank-1 LoRAs Encode Interpretable Reasoning Signals
papers.research_question: How can minimal parameter changes, specifically rank-1 LoRAs, be used to understand and interpret the mechanisms behind reasoning capabilities in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Minimal parameter changes via a rank-1 LoRA can recover most reasoning performance and provide interpretable insights, enabling targeted analysis of model behavior.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning capabilities in LLMs can be substantially recovered through minimal parameter modifications, and these changes encode interpretable, reasoning-specific signals, opening new avenues for understanding models via parameter-efficient methods.
papers.key_findings:
A rank-1 LoRA recovers 73-90% of reasoning benchmark performance compared to full finetuning.
LoRA activations are as interpretable as MLP neurons and fire for reasoning-specific behaviors.
Sparse autoencoder on LoRA activations identifies fine-grained, monosemantic features such as Mathematical Operators and Discourse Markers.
MLP adapters contribute more to performance changes than attention adapters, as shown by ablation studies.
The approach demonstrates that parameter-efficient methods can serve as a lens for mechanistic interpretability of reasoning models.
papers.limitation:
Trained on a small dataset (10 million tokens), which may not capture all circuits learned by models trained on larger datasets.
Inconclusive results from steering experiments; large steering magnitudes required, leading to model backtracking.
Heavy reliance on LLM-based autointerpretation methods, which may not uncover the true role of features.
Only one model (Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct) studied, and evaluation focused mostly on math-related reasoning benchmarks.
future_direction: Focused analysis identifying specific circuits that LoRAs interface with to illuminate core computational mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Reasoning models leverage inference-time compute to significantly enhance the performance of language models on difficult logical tasks, and have become a dominating paradigm in frontier LLMs. Despite their wide adoption, the mechanisms underpinning the enhanced performance of these reasoning models are not well understood. In this work, we show that the majority of new capabilities in reasoning models can be elicited by small, single-rank changes to base model parameters, with many of these changes being interpretable. Specifically, we use a rank-1 LoRA to create a minimal parameter adapter for Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct which recovers 73-90% of reasoning-benchmark performance compared to a full parameter finetune. We find that the activations of this LoRA are as interpretable as MLP neurons, and fire for reasoning-specific behaviors. Finally, we train a sparse autoencoder on the entire activation state of this LoRA and identify fine-grained and monosemantic features. Our findings highlight that reasoning performance can arise largely from minimal changes to base model parameters, and explore what these changes affect. More broadly, our work shows that parameter-efficient training methods can be used as a targeted lens for uncovering fundamental insights about language model behavior and dynamics.

papers.title: Video Prediction of Dynamic Physical Simulations With Pixel-Space Spatiotemporal Transformers
papers.research_question: This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts, focusing on causal modelling of physical simulations over time.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a simple, interpretable pure transformer model (PSViT) for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction in pixel-space, which extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% compared to existing latent-space approaches.
papers.conclusion: The presented simple, interpretable pure transformer for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction extends the horizon for physically accurate predictions while maintaining competitive performance on standard video quality metrics, highlighting the benefits of a straightforward end-to-end approach.
papers.key_findings:
The PSViT model achieves increased temporal accuracy in predicting PDE-driven video sequences compared to existing approaches, as measured by an object tracking metric.
The model maintains competitive performance on standard video quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR).
Interpretability experiments identify network regions that encode information useful for estimating PDE simulation parameters via probing.
The learned encoding of underlying physics generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters.
The model's performance is evaluated on several physics simulation datasets and common video prediction benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
For three of the simulation datasets increasing PSViT model size has minimal impact on performance over time.
For stochastic video-generation results on BAIR, the approach falls short compared to latent space models.
Object shapes, although positioned accurately, can distort over time, particularly when rotation is involved.
By performing end-to-end training, the model doesn't benefit from the large-scale pretrained image encoders/decoders often employed by latent space models.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated metrics for evaluating physical accuracy, moving beyond current object-based pixel distance methods.
Training larger models on higher-resolution datasets featuring increased visual fidelity and physical complexity.
papers.abstract: Inspired by the performance and scalability of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), transformer-based models have seen recent success in the visual domain. This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts. Focusing on causal modeling of physical simulations over time; a common shortcoming of existing video-generative approaches, we attempt to isolate spatiotemporal reasoning via physical object tracking metrics and unsupervised training on physical simulation datasets. We introduce a simple yet effective pure transformer model for autoregressive video prediction, utilizing continuous pixel-space representations for video prediction. Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Feature Interpretation Using Generative Adversarial Networks (FIGAN): A Framework for Visualizing a CNN’s Learned Features
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the features learned by a CNN to improve interpretability, especially for diffuse disease processes in medical imaging where current attribution methods are limited?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces FIGAN, a framework that uses a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize images that visualize the features learned by a CNN, providing global interpretability and clarifying ambiguities in existing attribution methods for medical imaging.
papers.conclusion: FIGAN is a useful tool for interpreting the features used by CNNs in medical imaging tasks, complementing current attribution methods by providing holistic, global interpretations that can improve model transparency and clinical acceptance.
papers.key_findings:
FIGAN generates synthetic image sequences that reveal the imaging features (e.g., cardiomegaly, vascular fullness) used by CNNs for regression and classification tasks in medical imaging.
The method can discriminate between different embedded features with distinct interpretations, such as vessel-liver contrast versus liver texture.
FIGAN produces meaningful feature interpretations even with small sample sizes (n=50), especially when using generator pretraining.
Incorporating auxiliary segmentations improves GAN performance and reduces boundary artifacts in synthetic images.
FIGAN's synthetic images help clarify the 'what' behind the 'where' highlighted by attribution maps like Grad-CAM.
papers.limitation:
GANs can be challenging to train, requiring hyperparameter tuning and ad-hoc strategies to prevent discriminator overfitting and GAN collapse.
FIGAN requires the source network to have satisfactory performance to ensure signal between the embedded features and the input images.
future_direction: Exploring methods to understand the manifestation of feature interactions in synthetic images.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are increasingly being explored and used for a variety of classification tasks in medical imaging, but current methods for post hoc explainability are limited. Most commonly used methods highlight portions of the input image that contribute to classification. While this provides a form of spatial localization relevant for focal disease processes, it may not be sufficient for co-localized or diffuse disease processes such as pulmonary edema or fibrosis. For the latter, new methods are required to isolate diffuse texture features employed by the CNN where localization alone is ambiguous. We therefore propose a novel strategy for eliciting explainability, called Feature Interpretation using Generative Adversarial Networks (FIGAN), which provides visualization of features used by a CNN for classification or regression. FIGAN uses a conditional generative adversarial network to synthesize images that span the range of a CNN’s principal embedded features. We apply FIGAN to two previously developed CNNs and show that the resulting feature interpretations can clarify ambiguities within attention areas highlighted by existing explainability methods. In addition, we perform a series of experiments to study the effect of auxiliary segmentations, training sample size, and image resolution on FIGAN’s ability to provide consistent and interpretable synthetic images.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Computer Vision
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ImageNet, a large-scale, clean, and diverse image database organized according to the WordNet hierarchy, providing a valuable resource for computer vision research.
papers.conclusion: ImageNet, with its scale, accuracy, diversity, and hierarchical structure, offers unparalleled opportunities for researchers in computer vision and beyond, and is expected to become a central resource for vision-related research.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet is significantly larger, more diverse, and more accurate than existing image datasets like TinyImage, ESP, Caltech101, and LabelMe.
The construction method using Amazon Mechanical Turk with a confidence-based voting scheme achieves an average labeling precision of 99.7% across different tree depths.
Exploiting the hierarchical structure of ImageNet with a simple tree-max classifier improves image classification performance compared to independent classifiers.
Using clean, full-resolution images from ImageNet with advanced feature representations (e.g., NBNN) leads to better object recognition performance compared to using noisy, low-resolution images.
ImageNet enables object localization and reveals intra-category diversity through clustering, showing variations in viewpoints and poses.
papers.limitation:
ImageNet currently does not provide segmentation annotations.
About 20% of synsets have very few images due to lack of web images or difficulty in illustration.
future_direction: Complete ImageNet to cover approximately 50,000 synsets with 50 million images.
Extend ImageNet to include more information such as localization, segmentation, cross-synset referencing, and expert annotation.
Use ImageNet as a training resource, benchmark dataset, and for introducing new semantic relations for visual modeling.
papers.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important in computer vision, aiming to connect complex model outputs with human understanding. This review provides a focused comparative analysis of representative XAI methods in four main categories, attribution-based, activation-based, perturbation-based, and transformer-based approaches, selected from a broader literature landscape. Attribution-based methods like Grad-CAM highlight key input regions using gradients and feature activation. Activation-based methods analyze the responses of internal neurons or feature maps to identify which parts of the input activate specific layers or units, helping to reveal hierarchical feature representations. Perturbation-based techniques, such as RISE, assess feature importance through input modifications without accessing internal model details. Transformer-based methods, which use self-attention, offer global interpretability by tracing information flow across layers. We evaluate these methods using metrics such as faithfulness, localization accuracy, efficiency, and overlap with medical annotations. We also propose a hierarchical taxonomy to classify these methods, reflecting the diversity of XAI techniques. Results show that RISE has the highest faithfulness but is computationally expensive, limiting its use in real-time scenarios. Transformer-based methods perform well in medical imaging, with high IoU scores, though interpreting attention maps requires care. These findings emphasize the need for context-aware evaluation and hybrid XAI methods balancing interpretability and efficiency. The review ends by discussing ethical and practical challenges, stressing the need for standard benchmarks and domain-specific tuning.

papers.title: Insight: Interpretable Semantic Hierarchies in Vision-Language Encoders
papers.research_question: How can we make language-aligned vision foundation models interpretable by decomposing their representations into human-interpretable, spatially grounded concepts?
papers.core_contribution: CFM is a concept foundation model that provides interpretable, spatially grounded concept representations for vision tasks, enabling explanations across classification, segmentation, and captioning.
papers.conclusion: CFM provides a unified concept representation for vision foundation models, yielding human-interpretable, spatially grounded concepts that maintain competitive task performance.
papers.key_findings:
CFM extracts concepts that are more localized, consistent, and pure than existing concept extraction methods.
CFM discovers explicit hierarchical relationships between concepts, improving interpretability.
CFM's concept representations enable competitive performance on downstream vision tasks while providing explanations.
CFM's concept naming is more accurate than baselines, especially when leveraging discovered hierarchies.
CFM enables interpretable open-vocabulary segmentation and steerable captioning through its concept bottleneck.
papers.limitation: Concept naming can be limited for fine-grained concepts, potentially due to the vocabulary not containing relevant names or misalignment between CLIP's text and image encoders.
papers.abstract: Language-aligned vision foundation models perform strongly across diverse downstream tasks. Yet, their learned representations remain opaque, making interpreting their decision-making hard. Recent works decompose these representations into human-interpretable concepts, but provide poor spatial grounding and are limited to image classification tasks. In this work, we propose Insight, a language-aligned concept foundation model that provides fine-grained concepts, which are human-interpretable and spatially grounded in the input image. We leverage a hierarchical sparse autoencoder and a foundation model with strong semantic representations to automatically extract concepts at various granularities. Examining local co-occurrence dependencies of concepts allows us to define concept relationships. Through these relations we further improve concept naming and obtain richer explanations. On benchmark data, we show that Insight provides performance on classification and segmentation that is competitive with opaque foundation models while providing fine-grained, high quality concept-based explanations. Code is available at https://github.com/kawi19/Insight.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: ConceptAttention: Diffusion Transformers Learn Highly Interpretable Features
papers.research_question: Do the rich representations of multi-modal diffusion transformers (DiTs) exhibit unique properties that enhance their interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CONCEPT ATTENTION, a method that repurposes DiT attention layers without training to produce high-quality saliency maps, and discovers that linear projections in the attention output space yield sharper maps than cross-attention maps.
papers.conclusion: Introduces CONCEPT ATTENTION, a method for interpreting the rich features of multi-modal DiTs, and suggests the potential for DiT models to act as powerful and interpretable image encoders with representations transferable zero-shot to tasks like image segmentation.
papers.key_findings:
CONCEPT ATTENTION produces high-quality saliency maps that precisely localize textual concepts within images.
