papers.conclusion: Transformers encode biomedical knowledge useful for inference, but careful evaluation is needed due to biases and information loss during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers like BioBERT and BioMegatron encode biomedical domain knowledge at entity and relational levels.
Fine-tuning for specific tasks can lead to loss of semantic information about entity types.
Clustering analysis shows that representations form biologically meaningful groups, such as genes from the same pathways.
Classification errors are correlated with the frequency of entities in the training data, indicating bias.
Despite strong evidence, some well-known clinical relations can be misclassified by the models.
papers.limitation: Models may misclassify well-known clinical relations due to biases in the dataset.
papers.abstract: Specialised transformers-based models (such as BioBERT and BioMegatron) are adapted for the biomedical domain based on publicly available biomedical corpora. As such, they have the potential to encode large-scale biological knowledge. We investigate the encoding and representation of biological knowledge in these models, and its potential utility to support inference in cancer precision medicine - namely, the interpretation of the clinical significance of genomic alterations. We compare the performance of different transformer baselines; we use probing to determine the consistency of encodings for distinct entities; and we use clustering methods to compare and contrast the internal properties of the embeddings for genes, variants, drugs and diseases. We show that these models do indeed encode biological knowledge, although some of this is lost in fine-tuning for specific tasks. Finally, we analyse how the models behave with regard to biases and imbalances in the dataset.

papers.title: Hierarchical Vision Transformer with Prototypes for Interpretable Medical Image Classification
papers.research_question: How can Vision Transformers be made more interpretable for medical image classification by integrating domain knowledge, hierarchical prediction, and prototype learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HierViT, a Vision Transformer with hierarchical structure and prototype learning for interpretable medical image classification, achieving high performance and human-aligned explanations.
papers.conclusion: HierViT advances Vision Transformers in explainable AI by leveraging domain knowledge and hierarchical architecture, providing intuitive reasoning similar to human experts and offering trustworthy interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
HierViT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIDC-IDRI dataset and comparable performance on the derm7pt dataset.
The model provides interpretable predictions through attribute scores, prototype images, and attention heatmaps.
Qualitative evaluation shows that attention heatmaps focus on clinically relevant regions for attribute assessment.
Prototype-based inference slightly reduces performance but enhances explainability by making prototypes causal for predictions.
Explanations can increase user confidence but may reduce human performance if the model's predictions are incorrect.
papers.limitation:
Scarcity of medical datasets with discrete annotations for predefined attributes.
Potential need to transfer attribute knowledge to similar radiological tasks.
Opportunities to enhance the architecture by integrating text processing or data synthesis.
future_direction: Transfer attribute knowledge to radiological diagnosis tasks with similar visual criteria.
Integrate a text processing branch to fuse information from radiology reports with image data.
Explore data synthesis to expand small-scale datasets using generative AI models conditioned on attributes.
papers.abstract: Explainability is a highly demanded requirement for applications in high-risk areas such as medicine. Vision Transformers have mainly been limited to attention extraction to provide insight into the model's reasoning. Our approach combines the high performance of Vision Transformers with the introduction of new explainability capabilities. We present HierViT, a Vision Transformer that is inherently interpretable and adapts its reasoning to that of humans. A hierarchical structure is used to process domain-specific features for prediction. It is interpretable by design, as it derives the target output with human-defined features that are visualized by exemplary images (prototypes). By incorporating domain knowledge about these decisive features, the reasoning is semantically similar to human reasoning and therefore intuitive. Moreover, attention heatmaps visualize the crucial regions for identifying each feature, thereby providing HierViT with a versatile tool for validating predictions. Evaluated on two medical benchmark datasets, LIDC-IDRI for lung nodule assessment and derm7pt for skin lesion classification, HierViT achieves superior and comparable prediction accuracy, respectively, while offering explanations that align with human reasoning.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Visual interpretability of image-based classification models by generative latent space disentanglement applied to in vitro fertilization
papers.research_question: How to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models in a human-interpretable way?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCOVER, a generative model that learns disentangled latent representations to discover and visualize the image properties driving classification decisions, enabling human-interpretable counterfactual explanations.
papers.conclusion: DISCOVER enables human-interpretable visual explanations for image classification models, discovers new image properties, and provides transparency for individual predictions, with potential for biological discovery.
papers.key_findings:
DISCOVER successfully identifies known blastocyst quality properties (size and trophectoderm) as classification-driving features.
DISCOVER discovers new properties (blastocoel density) that were not explicitly annotated.
DISCOVER provides instance-specific interpretation, ranking the importance of each property for individual predictions.
DISCOVER generalizes to other domains (natural images and Alzheimer's disease MRI).
DISCOVER outperforms existing interpretability methods (GradCAM, SHAP, LIME) in providing disentangled visual explanations.
papers.limitation:
One latent feature may encode multiple independent semantic image properties (entanglement).
DISCOVER may miss semantic image properties that are associated with the classification task (e.g., inner cell mass was not identified).
The method requires training a generative model, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The success of deep learning in identifying complex patterns exceeding human intuition comes at the cost of interpretability. Non-linear entanglement of image features makes deep learning a "black box" lacking human meaningful explanations for the models' decision. We present DISCOVER, a generative model designed to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models. DISCOVER learns disentangled latent representations, where each latent feature encodes a unique classification-driving visual property. This design enables "human-in-the-loop" interpretation by generating disentangled exaggerated counterfactual explanations. We apply DISCOVER to interpret classification of in vitro fertilization embryo morphology quality. We quantitatively and systematically confirm the interpretation of known embryo properties, discover properties without previous explicit measurements, and quantitatively determine and empirically verify the classification decision of specific embryo instances. We show that DISCOVER provides human-interpretable understanding of "black box" classification models, proposes hypotheses to decipher underlying biomedical mechanisms, and provides transparency for the classification of individual predictions.

papers.title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers build categorical representations for image classification, and how do self-attention and MLP layers contribute to this process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to project Vision Transformers' internal representations onto the class embedding space, enabling analysis of how class representations are built and the differential roles of self-attention and MLP layers via key-value memory pair mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework is a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability of Vision Transformers, providing insights into their category-building processes.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens develop class-specific representations from early stages, with class identifiability increasing across blocks.
Attention mechanisms and contextual information are crucial for building class representations; image tokens cannot develop class-identifiable representations in isolation.
Self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute: MLP layers promote strong categorical updates in late blocks, while self-attention layers promote weaker but more disseminated updates earlier.
The framework can identify image regions important for class detection and outperforms linear probing in revealing task-relevant features.
Key-value memory pair mechanisms in MLP and self-attention layers are involved in building class representations, with agreement rates correlating with model accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Only studies Vision Transformers trained for image classification.
Does not explore model editing or performance improvement applications.
future_direction: Adapt the framework to models with other types of output embeddings.
Use the mechanistic insights for model editing or performance improvement.
papers.abstract: Despite the growing use of transformer models in computer vision, a mechanistic understanding of these networks is still needed. This work introduces a method to reverse-engineer Vision Transformers trained to solve image classification tasks. Inspired by previous research in NLP, we demonstrate how the inner representations at any level of the hierarchy can be projected onto the learned class embedding space to uncover how these networks build categorical representations for their predictions. We use our framework to show how image tokens develop class-specific representations that depend on attention mechanisms and contextual information, and give insights on how self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute to this categorical composition. We additionally demonstrate that this method (1) can be used to determine the parts of an image that would be important for detecting the class of interest, and (2) exhibits significant advantages over traditional linear probing approaches. Taken together, our results position our proposed framework as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability research.

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Explainability Methods for Whole Slide Classification of Lymph Node Metastases using Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Which explainability method yields the best heatmaps for vision transformers in the histopathological context of whole slide image classification?
papers.core_contribution: Removal-based explainability methods, particularly ViT-Shapley, produce the most reliable and efficient heatmaps for vision transformers classifying lymph node metastases, outperforming attention-based and gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ViT-Shapley provides the best balance of trustworthiness and efficiency for explainability in clinical contexts, advocating for its adoption to understand and explain AI model decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Rollout methods produce overconfident artifacts and highlight non-informative regions like background.
Integrated Gradients focuses on a subset of individual tumor cells but performs poorly in quantitative metrics.
RISE and Shapley methods highlight areas covered by tumor cells, with Shapley showing the most concise heatmaps.
Removal-based methods (RISE and Shapley) significantly outperform others in Insertion and Deletion metrics.
ViT-Shapley is computationally more efficient than RISE, offering faster runtime for heatmap generation.
papers.limitation:
Insertion and Deletion metrics ignore the relativity of attribution with respect to ranked information and do not account for correlation between patches or network robustness.
The explainer training was limited to 10 epochs due to computational budget constraints.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Recent advancements in deep learning (DL), such as transformer networks, have shown promise in enhancing the performance of medical image analysis. In pathology, automated whole slide imaging (WSI) has transformed clinical workflows by streamlining routine tasks and diagnostic and prognostic support. However, the lack of transparency of DL models, often described as “black boxes”, poses a significant barrier to their clinical adoption. This necessitates the use of explainable AI methods (xAI) to clarify the decision-making processes of the models. Heatmaps can provide clinicians visual representations that highlight areas of interest or concern for the prediction of the specific model. Generating them from deep neural networks, especially from vision transformers, is non-trivial, as typically their self-attention mechanisms can lead to overconfident artifacts. The aim of this work is to evaluate current xAI methods for transformer models in order to assess which yields the best heatmaps in the histopathological context. Our study undertakes a comparative analysis for classifying a publicly available dataset comprising of N=400 WSIs of lymph node metastases of breast cancer patients. Our findings indicate that heatmaps calculated from Attention Rollout and Integrated Gradients are limited by artifacts and in quantitative performance. In contrast, removal-based methods like RISE and ViT-Shapley exhibit better qualitative attribution maps, showing better results in the well-known interpretability metrics for insertion and deletion. In addition, ViT-Shapley shows faster runtime and the most promising, reliable and practical heatmaps. Incorporating the heatmaps generated from approximate Shapley values in pathology reports could help to integrate xAI in the clinical workflow and increase trust in a scalable manner.

papers.title: DeepMiner: Discovering Interpretable Representations for Mammogram Classification and Explanation
papers.research_question: How to discover interpretable representations in deep neural networks and build explanations for medical predictions, specifically for mammogram classification.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DeepMiner, a human-in-the-loop framework for discovering interpretable representations in CNNs and generating explanations for medical predictions, specifically for mammogram classification.
papers.conclusion: DeepMiner is a framework that uncovers interpretable representations in deep neural networks and builds explanations for deep network predictions, and it is applicable to many other domains.
papers.key_findings:
Many individual units in the final convolutional layer of a CNN respond strongly to diseased tissue concepts specified by the BI-RADS lexicon.
DeepMiner can generate explanations for CNN mammogram classification that are consistent with ground truth radiology reports.
DeepMiner enables better understanding of the nuances of CNN classification decisions and possibly discovers new visual knowledge relevant to medical diagnosis.
future_direction: Generalization to other medical image classification tasks.
Incorporation of auxiliary features such as genetic information.
Potential for discovering unknown discriminative visual features for diseases less well understood than breast cancer.
papers.abstract: We propose DeepMiner, a framework to discover interpretable representations in deep neural networks and to build explanations for medical predictions. By probing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained to classify cancer in mammograms, we show that many individual units in the final convolutional layer of a CNN respond strongly to diseased tissue concepts specified by the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) lexicon. After expert annotation of the interpretable units, our proposed method is able to generate explanations for CNN mammogram classification that are consistent with ground truth radiology reports on the Digital Database for Screening Mammography. We show that DeepMiner not only enables better understanding of the nuances of CNN classification decisions but also possibly discovers new visual knowledge relevant to medical diagnosis.

papers.title: CytoSAE: Interpretable Cell Embeddings for Hematology
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied for interpretable morphological concept discovery in hematological imaging?
papers.core_contribution: CytoSAE is a sparse autoencoder that discovers interpretable morphological concepts in hematological images, generalizes across diverse and out-of-domain datasets, and enables explainable disease classification at patch, image, patient, and disease levels.
papers.conclusion: CytoSAE successfully learns interpretable morphological features across different hematological datasets, maintains generalizability to out-of-domain data, and enables multi-level analysis for interpretable disease classification.
papers.key_findings:
CytoSAE discovers morphologically relevant concepts that generalize across peripheral blood and bone marrow cytology datasets, validated by medical experts.
Patch-wise attribution allows sub-cellular level analysis of concepts, highlighting consistent morphological features across datasets.
Patient-level concept barcodes reveal disease-specific morphological features for AML subtypes, such as monocytic precursors for CBFB::MYH11 and granulated blasts for PML::RARA.
CytoSAE concepts achieve multi-class classification performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning methods while providing explainability.
Ablation studies show the number of discovered concepts is stable across expansion factors and hyperparameters, with optimal layers between 7–11 for concept balance.
papers.limitation: Manual expert validation was conducted only at the dataset level, not per patient, to avoid human selection bias in concept discovery.
future_direction: Explore patient-specific concept retrieval while minimizing subjectivity.
Incorporate semi-supervised learning techniques to refine the discovered features further.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerged as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based foundation models. Very recently, SAEs were also adopted for the visual domain, enabling the discovery of visual concepts and their patch-wise attribution to tokens in the transformer model. While a growing number of foundation models emerged for medical imaging, tools for explaining their inferences are still lacking. In this work, we show the applicability of SAEs for hematology. We propose CytoSAE, a sparse autoencoder which is trained on over 40,000 peripheral blood single-cell images. CytoSAE generalizes to diverse and out-of-domain datasets, including bone marrow cytology, where it identifies morphologically relevant concepts which we validated with medical experts. Furthermore, we demonstrate scenarios in which CytoSAE can generate patient-specific and disease-specific concepts, enabling the detection of pathognomonic cells and localized cellular abnormalities at the patch level. We quantified the effect of concepts on a patient-level AML subtype classification task and show that CytoSAE concepts reach performance comparable to the state-of-the-art, while offering explainability on the sub-cellular level. Source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/dynamical-inference/cytosae.

papers.title: Transformer Utilization in Medical Image Segmentation Networks
papers.research_question: What is the relative effectiveness of Transformer blocks in medical image segmentation networks, and are their representations replaceable by linear operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Transformer Ablation to quantify the effectiveness of Transformer blocks in medical image segmentation networks, finding that Transformer-learnt representations are often replaceable and that architectural design choices are crucial.
papers.conclusion: Transformer Ablation provides quantitative insights into the replaceability of Transformer-learnt representations in medical image segmentation networks, encouraging better network designs.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-learnt representations in medical image segmentation networks are often replaceable by linear operators when trained with convolutional or local attention components.
Transformer capacity alone cannot prevent representational replaceability and works in tandem with effective design.
The existence of explicit feature hierarchies in transformer blocks is more beneficial than the self-attention modules themselves.
Major spatial downsampling before Transformer modules in the bottleneck should be used with caution.
papers.abstract: Owing to success in the data-rich domain of natural images, Transformers have recently become popular in medical image segmentation. However, the pairing of Transformers with convolutional blocks in varying architectural permutations leaves their relative effectiveness to open interpretation. We introduce Transformer Ablations that replace the Transformer blocks with plain linear operators to quantify this effectiveness. With experiments on 8 models on 2 medical image segmentation tasks, we explore -- 1) the replaceable nature of Transformer-learnt representations, 2) Transformer capacity alone cannot prevent representational replaceability and works in tandem with effective design, 3) The mere existence of explicit feature hierarchies in transformer blocks is more beneficial than accompanying self-attention modules, 4) Major spatial downsampling before Transformer modules should be used with caution.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Microscopic Features of Tumor by Multi-task Adversarial CNNs To Improve Generalization
papers.research_question: How can we improve the generalization and transparency of CNNs in histopathology by guiding training to focus on clinically relevant features and discard confounding factors?
papers.core_contribution: A novel CNN architecture combining multi-task learning and adversarial training to learn interpretable, clinically relevant features and improve generalization in histopathology image analysis.
papers.conclusion: Expert knowledge can be proactively used during CNN training via additional tasks to drive representation learning, improving robustness, generalization, and transparency for histopathology applications.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed multi-task adversarial architecture achieves improved generalization with an average AUC of 0.89 vs. 0.86 baseline on breast cancer detection.
Linear probing confirms that interpretable pathology features (e.g., nuclei density) are learned by the model.
Uncertainty-based loss weighting provides stable training and robust performance across data shifts compared to vanilla weighting.
The adversarial branch for acquisition center did not show marked improvement, possibly due to inaccurate center labels.
High-order combinations of auxiliary tasks do not automatically yield better generalization than low-order ones.
papers.limitation:
The uncertainty estimated is only homoscedastic (task-dependent) and does not correspond to data-dependent main task uncertainty.
The choice of auxiliary tasks requires prior knowledge to ensure they cooperate with the main task.
The adversarial branch for acquisition center did not show marked improvement, possibly due to inaccurate center labels in some datasets.
Auxiliary tasks become harder to learn when scaled up in number, with lower R2 for individual feature regression.
future_direction: Explore unsupervised domain adaptation methods (e.g., domain alignment layers) to handle latent domain information.
Investigate different loss weighting strategies for the adversarial task and include other undesired control targets (e.g., rotation, scale).
Extract additional features from unlabeled data and introduce them as weak supervision during training.
papers.abstract: Adopting Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in the daily routine of primary diagnosis requires not only near-perfect precision, but also a sufficient degree of generalization to data acquisition shifts and transparency. Existing CNN models act as black boxes, not ensuring to the physicians that important diagnostic features are used by the model. Building on top of successfully existing techniques such as multi-task learning, domain adversarial training and concept-based interpretability, this paper addresses the challenge of introducing diagnostic factors in the training objectives. Here we show that our architecture, by learning end-to-end an uncertainty-based weighting combination of multi-task and adversarial losses, is encouraged to focus on pathology features such as density and pleomorphism of nuclei, e.g. variations in size and appearance, while discarding misleading features such as staining differences. Our results on breast lymph node tissue show significantly improved generalization in the detection of tumorous tissue, with best average AUC 0.89 (0.01) against the baseline AUC 0.86 (0.005). By applying the interpretability technique of linearly probing intermediate representations, we also demonstrate that interpretable pathology features such as nuclei density are learned by the proposed CNN architecture, confirming the increased transparency of this model. This result is a starting point towards building interpretable multi-task architectures that are robust to data heterogeneity. Our code is available at https://github.com/maragraziani/multitask_adversarial

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Expert identification of visual primitives used by CNNs during mammogram classification
papers.research_question: Can we create networks that explain their decision making? We seek to produce relevant and informative descriptions of the predictions made by a CNN in a format familiar to radiologists.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an expert-in-the-loop interpretation method to label the behavior of internal units in CNNs trained for mammogram classification, showing that many units detect visual patterns correlated with meaningful medical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: This exploratory study is an important first step towards interpreting the decisions made by CNNs in classification of diseased tissue, demonstrating that many CNN units identify meaningful medical phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Many CNN units identify recognizable medical phenomena used by radiologists, showing significant overlap with the BI-RADS lexicon.
Some units had no identified connection with breast cancer, and other units identified entangled events.
Networks trained to recognize cancer end up using many BI-RADS categories even though training labels were only positive/negative for cancer.
Units identify advanced cancers, large benign masses, calcifications, and important associated features such as spiculation, breast density, architectural distortions, and tissue near the nipple.
The network behavior could provide a new computational perspective on the relationship between breast density, tissue characteristics, and cancer risk.
papers.limitation: Some units had no identified connection with breast cancer, and yet other units identified entangled events.
papers.abstract: This work interprets the internal representations of deep neural networks trained for classification of diseased tissue in 2D mammograms. We propose an expert-in-the-loop inter- pretation method to label the behavior of internal units in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Expert radiologists identify that the visual patterns detected by the units are correlated with meaningful medical phenomena such as mass tissue and calcificated vessels. We demonstrate that several trained CNN models are able to produce explanatory descriptions to support the final classification decisions. We view this as an important first step toward interpreting the internal representations of medical classification CNNs and explaining their predictions.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Pre-processing and Compression: Understanding Hidden Representation Refinement Across Imaging Domains via Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How does the intrinsic dimension (ID) of a neural network's hidden representations change through its layers, and how does this behavior differ between natural and medical image domains?
papers.core_contribution: The progression of intrinsic dimension through network layers differs between natural and medical image models, with medical image models peaking earlier, and there is a strong correlation between the peak representation ID and the ID of the input data.
papers.conclusion: There are notable discrepancies in network behavior between natural and medical imaging domains regarding hidden representation information content, and the information content of a model's learned representations is guided by that of its training data.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimension of hidden representations typically first increases then decreases through network depth.
The peak of intrinsic dimension occurs earlier in medical image models (average relative depth 0.35) compared to natural image models (average relative depth 0.57).
There is a strong correlation (Pearson r=0.89) between the peak representation intrinsic dimension (dmax_repr) and the intrinsic dimension of the input data (ddata).
future_direction: Further probing the proposed connections between learned feature 'abstractness' and peak representation ID, such as by seeing if training for classification tasks with increasingly abstract super-classes results in an increased peak ID depth.
Attempting to disentangle the effects of dataset ID and feature 'abstractness' on peak representation ID using experiments that can control the precise ID of training data.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been interest in how geometric properties such as intrinsic dimension (ID) of a neural network's hidden representations change through its layers, and how such properties are predictive of important model behavior such as generalization ability. However, evidence has begun to emerge that such behavior can change significantly depending on the domain of the network's training data, such as natural versus medical images. Here, we further this inquiry by exploring how the ID of a network's learned representations changes through its layers, in essence, characterizing how the network successively refines the information content of input data to be used for predictions. Analyzing eleven natural and medical image datasets across six network architectures, we find that how ID changes through the network differs noticeably between natural and medical image models. Specifically, medical image models peak in representation ID earlier in the network, implying a difference in the image features and their abstractness that are typically used for downstream tasks in these domains. Additionally, we discover a strong correlation of this peak representation ID with the ID of the data in its input space, implying that the intrinsic information content of a model's learned representations is guided by that of the data it was trained on. Overall, our findings emphasize notable discrepancies in network behavior between natural and non-natural imaging domains regarding hidden representation information content, and provide further insights into how a network's learned features are shaped by its training data.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: This blog presents indirect evidence that induction heads, circuits in transformers that copy and complete patterns, may be the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests induction heads likely play a major role in in-context learning, though for large models the case is correlational and not conclusive.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form during a training phase change that coincides with a dramatic improvement in in-context learning.
Architectural perturbations that shift induction head formation also shift in-context learning improvements accordingly.
Ablating induction heads in small models significantly reduces in-context learning ability.
Induction heads can implement abstract behaviors like translation and pattern matching, suggesting generality beyond literal copying.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models is plausible for general in-context learning, and behaviors are continuous from small to large models.
papers.limitation: Evidence is preliminary and indirect, especially for large models, with potential confounds or alternative hypotheses.
future_direction: Future work could build on these results to establish the claim more firmly.
Studying phase changes up close may offer generalizable lessons for safety in machine learning systems.
papers.abstract: Do induction heads constitute the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer language models? This blog presents indirect evidence that induction heads, circuits in transformers that copy and complete patterns, may be the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models. The evidence suggests induction heads likely play a major role in in-context learning, though for large models the case is correlational and not conclusive.

papers.title: Mask-Free Neuron Concept Annotation for Interpreting Neural Networks in Medical Domain
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in medical domains without requiring pixel-wise annotated datasets for neuron concept annotation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MAMMI, a mask-free neuron concept annotation method for medical image models that uses vision-language models and adaptive selection to handle class imbalance, outperforming previous methods.
papers.conclusion: MAMMI is an effective mask-free method for neuron concept annotation in medical vision models, addressing limitations of previous approaches and demonstrating superior performance.
papers.key_findings:
MAMMI achieves superior performance in neuron concept annotation compared to mask-based and other vision-language methods in medical settings.
Using a medical-specific concept set extracted from MIMIC-CXR reports significantly improves interpretability over general concept sets.
Adaptive neuron representative image selection effectively handles class-imbalanced data distributions and improves concept matching.
MedCLIP outperforms other CLIP models for medical concept annotation in MAMMI.
MAMMI accurately identifies neuron concepts at penultimate layers, whereas baselines like TSI and CLIP Dissect fail to do so.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in deep neural networks have shown promise in aiding disease diagnosis and medical decision-making. However, ensuring transparent decision-making processes of AI models in compliance with regulations requires a comprehensive understanding of the model's internal workings. However, previous methods heavily rely on expensive pixel-wise annotated datasets for interpreting the model, presenting a significant drawback in medical domains. In this paper, we propose a novel medical neuron concept annotation method, named Mask-free Medical Model Interpretation (MAMMI), addresses these challenges. By using a vision-language model, our method relaxes the need for pixel-level masks for neuron concept annotation. MAMMI achieves superior performance compared to other interpretation methods, demonstrating its efficacy in providing rich representations for neurons in medical image analysis. Our experiments on a model trained on NIH chest X-rays validate the effectiveness of MAMMI, showcasing its potential for transparent clinical decision-making in the medical domain. The code is available at https://github.com/ailab-kyunghee/MAMMI.

papers.title: Using StyleGAN for Visual Interpretability of Deep Learning Models on Medical Images
papers.research_question: How can we provide more informative visual interpretability for black-box deep learning models on medical images, beyond just highlighting feature locations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new interpretability method that uses a trained StyleGAN to find directions in its latent space that change a black-box model's prediction, generating synthetic image transformations to show how features impact the prediction, providing more intuitive explanations than heatmap methods like GradCAM.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method provides an intuitive way to understand where predictive features are located in an image and how they impact the model's prediction, demonstrating that the models learned clinically relevant features in both experiments.
papers.key_findings:
The method shows the gradual emergence of clinically relevant osteoarthritis features (e.g., joint space narrowing, osteophytes) as the predicted severity increases, which aligns with biological progression.
On histology images, the method reveals the appearance of tumor cells and disappearance of lymphocytes as tumor probability increases, providing clinically meaningful explanations where GradCAM fails.
The method allows clinicians to build trust in model predictions, discover new biomarkers, and potentially reveal model biases.
The encoder-decoder model struggles to perfectly reconstruct histology images, likely due to under-represented data in the training set.
The method demonstrates that the underlying models (ResNet50) learned clinically relevant features for both tasks.
papers.limitation: The encoder-decoder model is not able to perfectly reconstruct histology images, possibly because the StyleGAN does not generate images that are under-represented in the training set.
papers.abstract: As AI-based medical devices are becoming more common in imaging fields like radiology and histology, interpretability of the underlying predictive models is crucial to expand their use in clinical practice. Existing heatmap-based interpretability methods such as GradCAM only highlight the location of predictive features but do not explain how they contribute to the prediction. In this paper, we propose a new interpretability method that can be used to understand the predictions of any black-box model on images, by showing how the input image would be modified in order to produce different predictions. A StyleGAN is trained on medical images to provide a mapping between latent vectors and images. Our method identifies the optimal direction in the latent space to create a change in the model prediction. By shifting the latent representation of an input image along this direction, we can produce a series of new synthetic images with changed predictions. We validate our approach on histology and radiology images, and demonstrate its ability to provide meaningful explanations that are more informative than GradCAM heatmaps. Our method reveals the patterns learned by the model, which allows clinicians to build trust in the model's predictions, discover new biomarkers and eventually reveal potential biases.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: MedSAE: Dissecting MedCLIP Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to improve interpretability of medical vision-language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Medical Sparse Autoencoders (MedSAEs) to extract interpretable, monosemantic features from MedCLIP embeddings, advancing mechanistic interpretability in medical vision.
papers.conclusion: This work presents a first step toward mechanistic interpretability in medical vision-language models, highlighting sparse autoencoders as a promising direction for building transparent, robust, and trustworthy medical AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
MedSAE neurons achieve lower entropy (2.25) than raw MedCLIP features (2.38), indicating higher monosemanticity.
21 medically meaningful features are identified with MedGEMMA-based automated naming, with detection accuracy above 70%.
MedSAE features show stronger alignment with clinical concepts compared to raw embeddings.
papers.limitation:
presence of inactive neurons and the need for more expressive SAE architectures
computational cost and dataset sensitivity of automated naming
limited validation across modalities and institutions
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence in healthcare requires models that are accurate and interpretable. We advance mechanistic interpretability in medical vision by applying Medical Sparse Autoencoders (MedSAEs) to the latent space of MedCLIP, a vision-language model trained on chest radiographs and reports. To quantify interpretability, we propose an evaluation framework that combines correlation metrics, entropy analyzes, and automated neuron naming via the MedGEMMA foundation model. Experiments on the CheXpert dataset show that MedSAE neurons achieve higher monosemanticity and interpretability than raw MedCLIP features. Our findings bridge high-performing medical AI and transparency, offering a scalable step toward clinically reliable representations.

papers.title: From Colors to Classes: Emergence of Concepts in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers (ViTs) process information layer by layer, and do they encode concepts with increasing complexity similar to convolutional neural networks (CNNs)?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers encode concepts with increasing complexity across layers, similar to CNNs, despite having global attention from the first layer. Finetuning reduces the number of encoded concepts and shifts them to task-relevant categories.
papers.conclusion: ViTs exhibit hierarchical feature extraction similar to CNNs, and concept-based analysis provides insights into their internal representations and the effects of pretraining and finetuning.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs encode more universal concepts (e.g., colors, textures) in early layers and more specialized concepts (e.g., objects, natural elements) in later layers.
Neurons in early layers activate on simpler images, while neurons in late layers react to more complex images.
Finetuning to specific downstream tasks reduces the number of encoded concepts and shifts concepts to task-relevant categories.
Different pretraining strategies influence the quantity and category of encoded concepts.
DINOv2 shows distinct behaviors, such as higher similarity scores and less concept change during finetuning, indicating better generalization.
papers.limitation:
The thresholding procedure uses a mean threshold per layer, which may suppress differences in interpretability between layers and models.
The categorization of concepts was done semi-automatically with LLMs and manual adjustments, which may contain subjective errors.
The definition of concepts as neuron labels assumes monosemanticity, but neurons can be polysemantic, so not all concepts may be captured.
future_direction: Developing a more reliable concept set and categorization for concept-based analysis.
Exploring the internal structures that enable models like DINOv2 to generalize well.
Investigating other methods of concept discovery for layer-wise analysis.
papers.abstract: Abstract Vision Transformers (ViTs) are increasingly utilized in various computer vision tasks due to their powerful representation capabilities. However, it remains understudied how ViTs process information layer by layer. Numerous studies have shown that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) extract features of increasing complexity throughout their layers, which is crucial for tasks like domain adaptation and transfer learning. ViTs, lacking the same inductive biases as CNNs, can potentially learn global dependencies from the first layers due to their attention mechanisms. Given the increasing importance of ViTs in computer vision, there is a need to improve the layer-wise understanding of ViTs. In this work, we present a novel, layer-wise analysis of concepts encoded in state-of-the-art ViTs using neuron labeling. Our findings reveal that ViTs encode concepts with increasing complexity throughout the network. Early layers primarily encode basic features such as colors and textures, while later layers represent more specific classes, including objects and animals. As the complexity of encoded concepts increases, the number of concepts represented in each layer also rises, reflecting a more diverse and specific set of features. Additionally, different pretraining strategies influence the quantity and category of encoded concepts, with finetuning to specific downstream tasks generally reducing the number of encoded concepts and shifting the concepts to more relevant categories.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Mammo-CLIP Dissect: A Framework for Analysing Mammography Concepts in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates: (1) how concept learning differs between DL vision models trained on general image datasets versus mammography-specific datasets; (2) how fine-tuning for downstream mammography tasks affects concept specialisation; and (3) which mammography-relevant concepts remain under-represented.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Mammo-CLIP Dissect, a concept-based explainability framework for dissecting deep learning vision models in mammography, and uses it to analyze how domain-specific training and fine-tuning affect concept learning.
papers.conclusion: Mammo-CLIP Dissect provides concept-level insights into how CNNs capture mammography-specific knowledge, moving beyond pixel-level interpretability toward an understanding aligned with radiologists' reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on mammography data capture more clinically relevant concepts and align more closely with radiologists' workflows.
Fine-tuning for task-specific classification enhances capture of certain concept categories (e.g., benign calcifications) but reduces coverage of others (e.g., density-related features).
Neurons show selective responsiveness to distinct mammography features such as implants and calcifications.
Mammo-CLIP Dissect reveals that domain-specific training leads to stronger and more stable alignment with mammography concepts.
The framework identifies under-represented concepts, including architectural distortion and modality-inappropriate terms.
papers.limitation: The concept set includes overlaps and modality-inappropriate concepts (e.g., from ultrasound or MRI) which may confound evaluation.
future_direction: Refining concept sets to reduce ambiguity.
Addressing subtle underrepresented findings.
Developing fine-tuning strategies that preserve general conceptual breadth while enhancing task-relevant features.
papers.abstract: Understanding what deep learning (DL) models learn is essential for the safe deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical settings. While previous work has focused on pixel-based explainability methods, less attention has been paid to the textual concepts learned by these models, which may better reflect the reasoning used by clinicians. We introduce Mammo-CLIP Dissect, the first concept-based explainability framework for systematically dissecting DL vision models trained for mammography. Leveraging a mammography-specific vision-language model (Mammo-CLIP) as a "dissector," our approach labels neurons at specified layers with human-interpretable textual concepts and quantifies their alignment to domain knowledge. Using Mammo-CLIP Dissect, we investigate three key questions: (1) how concept learning differs between DL vision models trained on general image datasets versus mammography-specific datasets; (2) how fine-tuning for downstream mammography tasks affects concept specialisation; and (3) which mammography-relevant concepts remain underrepresented. We show that models trained on mammography data capture more clinically relevant concepts and align more closely with radiologists' workflows than models not trained on mammography data. Fine-tuning for task-specific classification enhances the capture of certain concept categories (e.g., benign calcifications) but can reduce coverage of others (e.g., density-related features), indicating a trade-off between specialisation and generalisation. Our findings show that Mammo-CLIP Dissect provides insights into how convolutional neural networks (CNNs) capture mammography-specific knowledge. By comparing models across training data and fine-tuning regimes, we reveal how domain-specific training and task-specific adaptation shape concept learning. Code and concept set are available: https://github.com/Suaiba/Mammo-CLIP-Dissect.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: A Simple Interpretable Transformer for Fine-Grained Image Classification and Analysis
papers.research_question: How can we design an interpretable image classification model that proactively searches for class-specific patterns in an image using a Transformer architecture?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces INTR, an interpretable Transformer for image classification that uses class-specific queries to generate cross-attention maps, providing faithful interpretations without post-hoc methods.
papers.conclusion: INTR is a simple, interpretable Transformer that can localize attributes for fine-grained classification and has potential for scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
INTR learns to produce distinct cross-attention weights for each class, providing faithful interpretations.
Multi-head cross-attention in INTR can identify different attributes of a class, making it suitable for fine-grained classification.
INTR achieves comparable accuracy to ResNet-50 on most fine-grained datasets.
INTR's attention maps are more discriminative and sharper than post-hoc methods like Grad-CAM and RISE.
INTR can identify shared and discriminative attributes in similar classes.
papers.limitation:
INTR's accuracy drops on datasets with complex backgrounds or small objects, such as CUB.
INTR only handles static images and cannot analyze behavior from videos.
future_direction: Extending INTR to videos to analyze behavior.
Applying INTR to other modalities and tasks.
papers.abstract: We present a novel usage of Transformers to make image classification interpretable. Unlike mainstream classifiers that wait until the last fully connected layer to incorporate class information to make predictions, we investigate a proactive approach, asking each class to search for itself in an image. We realize this idea via a Transformer encoder-decoder inspired by DEtection TRansformer (DETR). We learn "class-specific" queries (one for each class) as input to the decoder, enabling each class to localize its patterns in an image via cross-attention. We name our approach INterpretable TRansformer (INTR), which is fairly easy to implement and exhibits several compelling properties. We show that INTR intrinsically encourages each class to attend distinctively; the cross-attention weights thus provide a faithful interpretation of the prediction. Interestingly, via "multi-head" cross-attention, INTR could identify different "attributes" of a class, making it particularly suitable for fine-grained classification and analysis, which we demonstrate on eight datasets. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly accessible at the Imageomics Institute GitHub site: https://github.com/Imageomics/INTR.

papers.title: What do Vision Transformers Learn? A Visual Exploration
papers.research_question: What do vision transformers learn and how do they differ from convolutional neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a visualization framework for ViTs and finds that ViTs preserve spatial information except in the last layer, use background information more effectively than CNNs, and with language supervision learn semantic concepts.
papers.conclusion: ViTs learn spatial relationships from scratch and their last layer performs token mixing similar to average pooling; ViTs and CNNs share similarities in feature progression but differ in use of background and high-frequency information.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs preserve spatial information in all layers except the last layer, which behaves like a learned global pooling operation.
ViTs make better use of background information than CNNs and are less reliant on high-frequency texture information.
ViTs show a progression from edges/textures to parts to objects in deeper layers, similar to CNNs.
ViTs trained with CLIP learn features corresponding to abstract concepts and linguistic elements (prepositions, adjectives, etc.).
The feed-forward layer in ViTs is more interpretable for visualization than keys, queries, and values.
papers.limitation: Visualization method fails for low-dimensional components like keys, queries, and values due to feature entanglement
papers.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) are quickly becoming the de-facto architecture for computer vision, yet we understand very little about why they work and what they learn. While existing studies visually analyze the mechanisms of convolutional neural networks, an analogous exploration of ViTs remains challenging. In this paper, we first address the obstacles to performing visualizations on ViTs. Assisted by these solutions, we observe that neurons in ViTs trained with language model supervision (e.g., CLIP) are activated by semantic concepts rather than visual features. We also explore the underlying differences between ViTs and CNNs, and we find that transformers detect image background features, just like their convolutional counterparts, but their predictions depend far less on high-frequency information. On the other hand, both architecture types behave similarly in the way features progress from abstract patterns in early layers to concrete objects in late layers. In addition, we show that ViTs maintain spatial information in all layers except the final layer. In contrast to previous works, we show that the last layer most likely discards the spatial information and behaves as a learned global pooling operation. Finally, we conduct large-scale visualizations on a wide range of ViT variants, including DeiT, CoaT, ConViT, PiT, Swin, and Twin, to validate the effectiveness of our method.
