Hybrid-k routing (language-specific experts with cross-lingual routing) outperforms Top-k and Language-Specific routing.
papers.abstract: Adapting medical Large Language Models to local languages can reduce barriers to accessing healthcare services, but data scarcity remains a significant challenge, particularly for low-resource languages. To address this, we first construct a high-quality medical dataset and conduct analysis to ensure its quality. In order to leverage the generalization capability of multilingual LLMs to efficiently scale to more resource-constrained languages, we explore the internal information flow of LLMs from a multilingual perspective using Mixture of Experts (MoE) modularity. Technically, we propose a novel MoE routing method that employs language-specific experts and cross-lingual routing. Inspired by circuit theory, our routing analysis revealed a Spread Out in the End information flow mechanism: while earlier layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, the later layers exhibit language-specific divergence. This insight directly led to the development of the Post-MoE architecture, which applies sparse routing only in the later layers while maintaining dense others. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances the generalization of multilingual models to other languages while preserving interpretability. Finally, to efficiently scale the model to 50 languages, we introduce the concept of language family experts, drawing on linguistic priors, which enables scaling the number of languages without adding additional parameters.

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user’s desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: Explaining Chest X-ray Pathology Models using Textual Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we explain black-box medical image classifiers using textual concepts without requiring manually annotated concept datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CoCoX, a method that leverages a vision-language model's joint embedding space to generate conceptual counterfactual explanations for chest X-ray pathology classifiers without needing annotated concept data.
papers.conclusion: CoCoX provides clinically relevant conceptual explanations for chest X-ray pathology classifiers and can be extended to other medical imaging domains with domain-specific concept banks.
papers.key_findings:
CoCoX generates top concepts that align with clinically relevant features for pathologies like Cardiomegaly, Pleural Effusion, and Atelectasis.
The method achieves high recall for primary clinical findings but lower recall for secondary findings, which are more numerous and include non-visual attributes.
CoCoX generates explanations faster than the baseline method CheXplaining in Style.
The approach works across different classifier architectures (DenseNet121, ResNet34, VLM+Linear).
The concept bank can be easily augmented with new textual concepts without requiring annotated images.
papers.limitation: Concepts such as 'Older patients' in the secondary list for Cardiomegaly and Atelectasis are non-visual attributes and challenging to generate conceptual counterfactuals for.
future_direction: Extending the method to other medical imaging domains (e.g., MRI or CT scans) with tailored concept banks.
Exploring ways to improve concept bank creation.
Exploring standardized metrics like expert consensus scores and counterfactual faithfulness in future iterations.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have revolutionized medical imaging and diagnostics, yet their opaque nature poses challenges for clinical adoption and trust. Amongst approaches to improve model interpretability, concept-based explanations aim to provide concise and human-understandable explanations of any arbitrary classifier. However, such methods usually require a large amount of manually collected data with concept annotation, which is often scarce in the medical domain. In this paper, we propose Conceptual Counterfactual Explanations for Chest X-ray (CoCoX), which leverages the joint embedding space of an existing vision-language model (VLM) to explain black-box classifier outcomes without the need for annotated datasets. Specifically, we utilize textual concepts derived from chest radiography reports and a pre-trained chest radiography-based VLM to explain three common cardiothoracic pathologies. We demonstrate that the explanations generated by our method are semantically meaningful and faithful to underlying pathologies.

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: Studying Cross-cluster Modularity in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of training neural networks to be modular using a clusterability loss on interpretability, such as task specialization and circuit size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a clusterability measure and loss function to train neural networks to be modular. Shows that modular models do not exhibit more task specialization but have smaller circuits, aiding interpretability.
papers.conclusion: A simple regularizer can split neural network layers into non-interacting modules, but these modules do not yield expected interpretability benefits like task specialization. However, modularity improves circuit size and search space without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models are not modular; clusters are highly enmeshed.
Training with clusterability loss effectively increases modularity in models.
Modular models do not show increased task specialization compared to non-modular models.
Modular models have smaller effective circuits, reducing circuit size.
Theoretical analysis indicates modularity simplifies function spaces and reduces the number of features.
papers.limitation: The modularity metric does not lead to clear interpretability benefits such as task specialization.
future_direction: Investigate alternative regularizers for interpretability benefits.
Build an automated subtask detection mechanism.
papers.abstract: An approach to improve neural network interpretability is via clusterability, i.e., splitting a model into disjoint clusters that can be studied independently. We define a measure for clusterability and show that pre-trained models form highly enmeshed clusters via spectral graph clustering. We thus train models to be more modular using a "clusterability loss" function that encourages the formation of non-interacting clusters. We then investigate the emerging properties of these highly clustered models. We find our trained clustered models do not exhibit more task specialization, but do form smaller circuits. We investigate CNNs trained on MNIST and CIFAR, small transformers trained on modular addition, and GPT-2 and Pythia on the Wiki dataset, and Gemma on a Chemistry dataset. This investigation shows what to expect from clustered models.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Interpretability-Aware Pruning for Efficient Medical Image Analysis
papers.research_question: How can interpretability techniques be used to guide pruning of neural networks to reduce model complexity while preserving predictive performance and transparency in medical image analysis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability-guided pruning framework that leverages attribution methods to prune neurons, achieving high compression rates with minimal accuracy loss for medical image models.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-guided pruning offers an effective pathway to building lightweight, interpretable, and potentially more robust AI systems for deployment in high-stakes domains like healthcare.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability-guided pruning enables high model compression while maintaining accuracy within a 5% margin across datasets and architectures.
Vision Transformers (ViTs) show exceptional robustness to pruning, preserving performance even beyond 65-80% pruning rates.
Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) consistently achieves the highest pruning thresholds with the lowest accuracy drop compared to DL-Backtrace and Integrated Gradients.
Clustering-based sampling for importance computation outperforms confidence-based and random sampling, providing more robust pruning results.
Pruning can sometimes improve accuracy by removing neurons with negative or noisy influence, enhancing generalization.
future_direction: Pruning pre-trained models using region-specific, representative data to improve generalization at deployment.
papers.abstract: Deep learning has driven significant advances in medical image analysis, yet its adoption in clinical practice remains constrained by the large size and lack of transparency in modern models. Advances in interpretability techniques such as DL-Backtrace, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, and Integrated Gradients make it possible to assess the contribution of individual components within neural networks trained on medical imaging tasks. In this work, we introduce an interpretability-guided pruning framework that reduces model complexity while preserving both predictive performance and transparency. By selectively retaining only the most relevant parts of each layer, our method enables targeted compression that maintains clinically meaningful representations. Experiments across multiple medical image classification benchmarks demonstrate that this approach achieves high compression rates with minimal loss in accuracy, paving the way for lightweight, interpretable models suited for real-world deployment in healthcare settings.

papers.title: Restyling Unsupervised Concept Based Interpretable Networks with Generative Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve the visualization and interpretation of learnt unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks for large-scale images?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VisCoIN, a novel architecture for unsupervised concept-based interpretable networks that maps concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model, enabling high-quality visualization and interactive interpretation of learnt concepts.
papers.conclusion: VisCoIN effectively leverages pretrained generative models to improve visualization and interpretation of unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks, achieving high prediction performance and learning more faithful and consistent concepts.
papers.key_findings:
VisCoIN achieves comparable prediction accuracy to baseline methods while improving reconstruction fidelity and perceptual similarity.
The learnt concepts in VisCoIN are more faithful and consistent compared to previous unsupervised CoINs.
The visualization pipeline based on the generative model allows for granular and interactive interpretation of concepts by modifying concept activations and observing changes in generated images.
papers.limitation:
Cannot guarantee that concepts precisely correspond to human concepts and may encode additional information.
System quality is limited by the quality of the pretrained generative model.
Linear trajectories in latent space may not be optimal for latent traversals.
papers.abstract: Developing inherently interpretable models for prediction has gained prominence in recent years. A subclass of these models, wherein the interpretable network relies on learning high-level concepts, are valued because of closeness of concept representations to human communication. However, the visualization and understanding of the learnt unsupervised dictionary of concepts encounters major limitations, especially for large-scale images. We propose here a novel method that relies on mapping the concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model. The use of a generative model enables high quality visualization, and lays out an intuitive and interactive procedure for better interpretation of the learnt concepts by imputing concept activations and visualizing generated modifications. Furthermore, leveraging pretrained generative models has the additional advantage of making the training of the system more efficient. We quantitatively ascertain the efficacy of our method in terms of accuracy of the interpretable prediction network, fidelity of reconstruction, as well as faithfulness and consistency of learnt concepts. The experiments are conducted on multiple image recognition benchmarks for large-scale images. Project page available at https://jayneelparekh.github.io/VisCoIN_project_page/

papers.title: Deeper Insights Without Updates: The Power of In-Context Learning Over Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning capture implicit patterns better than fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns in tasks, and the authors propose circuit shift theory to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning significantly outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns within specific tasks and exhibits greater adaptability in problem-solving approaches, as evidenced by notable shifts in model circuits.
papers.key_findings:
ICL achieves higher accuracy than fine-tuning on implicit pattern detection tasks across models and tasks.
ICL is more robust to misleading data and out-of-distribution data compared to fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning plateaus quickly with more data, showing diminishing returns for implicit pattern detection.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods do not show significant improvement over full-parameter fine-tuning for implicit pattern detection.
ICL induces larger circuit shifts than fine-tuning, indicating a more significant change in the model's problem-solving approach.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is constrained by the specific nature of the implicit pattern detection tasks, limited to certain domains.
Circuit Shift analysis relies on activation patching and sensitivity analysis, which require further refinement and validation across different models and tasks.
Computational resources required for fine-tuning, especially with large models, may limit the feasibility of such experiments in broader settings.
A detailed cost-benefit analysis comparing ICL and fine-tuning in terms of computational efficiency and performance is needed.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning and in-context learning (ICL) are two prevalent methods in imbuing large language models with task-specific knowledge. It is commonly believed that fine-tuning can surpass ICL given sufficient training samples as it allows the model to adjust its internal parameters based on the data. However, this paper presents a counterintuitive finding: For tasks with implicit patterns, ICL captures these patterns significantly better than fine-tuning. We developed several datasets featuring implicit patterns, such as sequences determining answers through parity or identifying reducible terms in calculations. We then evaluated the models' understanding of these patterns under both fine-tuning and ICL across models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The results indicate that models employing ICL can quickly grasp deep patterns and significantly improve accuracy. In contrast, fine-tuning, despite utilizing thousands of times more training samples than ICL, achieved only limited improvements. We also proposed circuit shift theory from a mechanistic interpretability's view to explain why ICL wins.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: The Inductive Bottleneck: Data-Driven Emergence of Representational Sparsity in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Is the inductive bottleneck (U-shaped entropy profile) in Vision Transformers an inherent property of the Self-Attention mechanism, or a dynamic reaction to the statistical properties of the training data?
papers.core_contribution: The inductive bottleneck (U-shaped entropy profile) in Vision Transformers is not an architectural artifact but a data-dependent adaptation that correlates with the semantic abstraction required by the task.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bottleneck is a data-driven emergence of representational sparsity in Vision Transformers, demonstrating that ViTs are dynamic hierarchy networks that build their own bottlenecks on demand.
papers.key_findings:
The depth of the bottleneck correlates strongly with the semantic abstraction required by the task.
For texture-heavy datasets (UC Merced), the network maintains high-rank representations throughout all layers.
For object-centric datasets (CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet), the network compresses information in middle layers to isolate semantic features.
The bottleneck is an active compression mechanism learned by the network.
Vanilla ViTs can emulate hierarchical compression like Swin Transformers but in a flexible, data-dependent manner.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to ViT-Small; it is unclear if larger models exhibit the same relative percentages.
The study focused on Classification/DINO; it is unclear if Dense Prediction tasks (Segmentation, Detection) would prevent bottleneck formation.
No causal intervention (e.g., forcing low rank) was performed to test if the bottleneck improves performance.
future_direction: Explore if ViT-Large or ViT-Huge exhibit the same relative percentages or add more 'Phantom Dimensions'.
Investigate if Dense Prediction tasks (Segmentation, Detection) prevent bottleneck formation.
Perform causal intervention (e.g., forcing low rank) to see if it improves performance, and explore 'Spectral Pruning' during training.
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) lack the hierarchical inductive biases inherent to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), theoretically allowing them to maintain high-dimensional representations throughout all layers. However, recent observations suggest ViTs often spontaneously manifest a "U-shaped" entropy profile-compressing information in middle layers before expanding it for the final classification. In this work, we demonstrate that this "Inductive Bottleneck" is not an architectural artifact, but a data-dependent adaptation. By analyzing the layer-wise Effective Encoding Dimension (EED) of DINO-trained ViTs across datasets of varying compositional complexity (UC Merced, Tiny ImageNet, and CIFAR-100), we show that the depth of the bottleneck correlates strongly with the semantic abstraction required by the task. We find that while texture-heavy datasets preserve high-rank representations throughout, object-centric datasets drive the network to dampen high-frequency information in middle layers, effectively "learning" a bottleneck to isolate semantic features.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is in-context learning (ICL) in transformers a persistent phenomenon, or does it emerge and then disappear (become transient) during training?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning (ICL) in transformers is often transient: it emerges and then disappears during training, even as training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for in-weights learning (IWL).
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is often transient, emphasizing the importance of validation metrics, early stopping, or regularization to preserve ICL capabilities during training.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges and then disappears (is transient) during training, while IWL accuracy increases.
ICL transience occurs across a range of model sizes (depth, embedding dimension), dataset sizes (number of classes, exemplars per class), and dataset types (Omniglot images, LLaMa token embeddings).
Data distributional properties, such as a larger number of classes or a Zipfian skew, can postpone the transience of ICL.
L2 regularization can mitigate or eliminate ICL transience, potentially by favoring the lower-norm ICL circuit.
Preliminary evidence suggests ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits for resources in the transformer's residual stream.
future_direction: Explore the effect of alternate optimizers or initialization schemes on the transience of ICL.
Connect findings to natural language settings and large-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks can exhibit a surprising capacity for in-context learning (ICL) despite not being explicitly trained for it. Prior work has provided a deeper understanding of how ICL emerges in transformers, e.g. through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, Bayesian inference, or by examining the distributional properties of training data. However, in each of these cases, ICL is treated largely as a persistent phenomenon; namely, once ICL emerges, it is assumed to persist asymptotically. Here, we show that the emergence of ICL during transformer training is, in fact, often transient. We train transformers on synthetic data designed so that both ICL and in-weights learning (IWL) strategies can lead to correct predictions. We find that ICL first emerges, then disappears and gives way to IWL, all while the training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for IWL. The transient nature of ICL is observed in transformers across a range of model sizes and datasets, raising the question of how much to "overtrain" transformers when seeking compact, cheaper-to-run models. We find that L2 regularization may offer a path to more persistent ICL that removes the need for early stopping based on ICL-style validation tasks. Finally, we present initial evidence that ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Illuminated Decision Trees with Lucid
papers.research_question: How can feature visualization methods be applied to classifiers trained on visually simple but challenging tasks, and can they be combined with decision trees for better interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Illuminated Decision Tree method, which uses a CNN as a feature extractor, learns a decision tree on these features, and provides Lucid visualizations for each tree node to enhance interpretability for challenging image classification tasks.
papers.conclusion: The Illuminated Decision Tree approach provides a way to make CNN-based classifiers more interpretable, useful for model development, debugging, and explaining outputs to non-experts, especially for visually simple but challenging tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Feature visualizations for white blood cell classification show similar patterns to more complex datasets, with lower layers capturing simple features and higher layers capturing more abstract structures.
The Illuminated Decision Tree approach can create interpretable classifiers with only a small reduction in accuracy compared to the original CNN.
The method helps identify biases in the training data, such as the classifier focusing on background features rather than the cells of interest.
For the easier classification task (lymphocytes vs. eosinophils), the decision tree uses features that correspond to human-interpretable colors, like pink for eosinophils.
For the more difficult task (eosinophils vs. neutrophils), the features are more complex and less discriminative, reflecting the challenge of the task.
papers.limitation:
Feature visualizations for simple datasets like white blood cells can be difficult to interpret beyond overall color.
The approach may not scale well to tasks with many classes, as decision trees become uninterpretable with many branches.
papers.abstract: The Lucid methods described by Olah et al. (2018) provide a way to inspect the inner workings of neural networks trained on image classification tasks using feature visualization. Such methods have generally been applied to networks trained on visually rich, large-scale image datasets like ImageNet, which enables them to produce enticing feature visualizations. To investigate these methods further, we applied them to classifiers trained to perform the much simpler (in terms of dataset size and visual richness), yet challenging task of distinguishing between different kinds of white blood cell from microscope images. Such a task makes generating useful feature visualizations difficult, as the discriminative features are inherently hard to identify and interpret. We address this by presenting the "Illuminated Decision Tree" approach, in which we use a neural network trained on the task as a feature extractor, then learn a decision tree based on these features, and provide Lucid visualizations for each node in the tree. We demonstrate our approach with several examples, showing how this approach could be useful both in model development and debugging, and when explaining model outputs to non-experts.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Weight Decay Improves Language Model Plasticity
papers.research_question: How does weight decay during language model pretraining affect model plasticity, i.e., the pretrained model’s ability to learn new knowledge during subsequent training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that weight decay during pretraining improves model plasticity, leading to better downstream performance after fine-tuning, and that optimizing pretraining hyperparameters solely for validation loss may not yield the best downstream model.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates the importance of using evaluation metrics beyond cross-entropy loss for hyperparameter optimization and casts light on the multifaceted role that a single optimization hyperparameter plays in shaping model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay improves language model plasticity and downstream performance.
The optimal pretraining weight decay for downstream performance is larger than the default of 0.1.
Pretraining validation loss is not perfectly predictive of downstream performance after fine-tuning.
Weight decay encourages linearly separable representations in the model.
Weight decay reduces the rank of attention matrices and reduces overfitting on training data.
papers.limitation:
The benefits of increased plasticity must be weighed against other effects that may depend on model size, training duration, and other parameters of the training setup.
In heavily overtrained scenarios or for very large models, the benefits of lower pretraining validation loss may outweigh those of plasticity.
future_direction: Investigate trade-offs between stability and plasticity and the extent to which results hold in large-model and heavily overtrained scenarios.
Investigate the role of weight decay in model plasticity for foundation models beyond language (e.g., multimodal foundation models).
Investigate the role of weight decay for other downstream desiderata (e.g., safety alignment).
papers.abstract: The prevailing paradigm in large language model (LLM) development is to pretrain a base model, then perform further training to improve performance and model behavior. However, hyperparameter optimization and scaling laws have been studied primarily from the perspective of the base model's validation loss, ignoring downstream adaptability. In this work, we study pretraining from the perspective of model plasticity, that is, the ability of the base model to successfully adapt to downstream tasks through fine-tuning. We focus on the role of weight decay, a key regularization parameter during pretraining. Through systematic experiments, we show that models trained with larger weight decay values are more plastic, meaning they show larger performance gains when fine-tuned on downstream tasks. This phenomenon can lead to counterintuitive trade-offs where base models that perform worse after pretraining can perform better after fine-tuning. Further investigation of weight decay's mechanistic effects on model behavior reveals that it encourages linearly separable representations, regularizes attention matrices, and reduces overfitting on the training data. In conclusion, this work demonstrates the importance of using evaluation metrics beyond cross-entropy loss for hyperparameter optimization and casts light on the multifaceted role of that a single optimization hyperparameter plays in shaping model behavior.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Is Grad-CAM Explainable in Medical Images?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the explainability of Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) in medical imaging applications, focusing on its ability to enhance interpretability and trust in deep learning models.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates the application of Grad-CAM for explainable deep learning in medical image analysis, showing its utility in visualizing decision-making processes for cancer detection.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM shows promise for enhancing interpretability in medical imaging, though further research is needed to improve accuracy and extend to other modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM provides visual explanations that highlight important regions in medical images for classification decisions.
The implemented model using densenet169 achieves an accuracy of 96.7% on the metastasis detection task.
papers.limitation: Grad-CAM has limitations including lack of robustness to changes in input image and unclear explanation of the basis for prediction in complex images.
future_direction: Improving the accuracy of Grad-CAM visualizations.
Extending Grad-CAM to other medical imaging modalities.
Developing user interfaces for intuitive visualization of model decisions for clinicians.
papers.abstract: Explainable Deep Learning has gained significant attention in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in domains such as medical imaging, where accurate and interpretable machine learning models are crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment planning. Grad-CAM is a baseline that highlights the most critical regions of an image used in a deep learning model's decision-making process, increasing interpretability and trust in the results. It is applied in many computer vision (CV) tasks such as classification and explanation. This study explores the principles of Explainable Deep Learning and its relevance to medical imaging, discusses various explainability techniques and their limitations, and examines medical imaging applications of Grad-CAM. The findings highlight the potential of Explainable Deep Learning and Grad-CAM in improving the accuracy and interpretability of deep learning models in medical imaging. The code is available in (will be available).

papers.title: Interpretable Image Recognition with Hierarchical Prototypes
papers.research_question: How can vision models be made interpretable by using hierarchically organized prototypes to classify objects at every level in a predefined taxonomy, and how can such models interpretably classify images from previously unseen classes at the appropriate taxonomic level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces HPnet, a model that uses hierarchically organized prototypes to classify objects at every level in a predefined taxonomy, providing distinct explanations for predictions at each level and enabling interpretable classification of images from previously unseen classes at the appropriate taxonomic level.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a model that classifies objects at each level in a semantic taxonomy, identifies when objects are novel at fine-grained levels, and uses directly interpretable features tailored to each parent node in the taxonomy, demonstrating the viability of the method on ImageNet.
papers.key_findings:
HPnet performs similarly to its black-box counterpart (VGG-16) and its flat prototype counterpart (Pnet) on fine-grained and coarse-grained classification tasks.
The model can correctly classify novel data at the coarse level at far above the chance rate (62.16% accuracy).
The learned prototypes encode meaningful visual features (e.g., wheels for vehicles) and the latent space exhibits good clustering quality, with prototypes surrounded by patch vectors from images of the correct class.
The model provides interpretable explanations for classifications at each taxonomic level via prototype activation heatmaps.
There is a trade-off between interpretability and accuracy, with HPnet showing a 2.32% drop in fine-grained accuracy compared to the VGG-16 model it was initialized from.
papers.limitation: There is a drop in fine-grained accuracy (2.32%) compared to the black-box VGG-16 model due to the constraints introduced for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Vision models are interpretable when they classify objects on the basis of features that a person can directly understand. Recently, methods relying on visual feature prototypes have been developed for this purpose. However, in contrast to how humans categorize objects, these approaches have not yet made use of any taxonomical organization of class labels. With such an approach, for instance, we may see why a chimpanzee is classified as a chimpanzee, but not why it was considered to be a primate or even an animal. In this work we introduce a model that uses hierarchically organized prototypes to classify objects at every level in a predefined taxonomy. Hence, we may find distinct explanations for the prediction an image receives at each level of the taxonomy. The hierarchical prototypes enable the model to perform another important task: interpretably classifying images from previously unseen classes at the level of the taxonomy to which they correctly relate, e.g. classifying a hand gun as a weapon, when the only weapons in the training data are rifles. With a subset of ImageNet, we test our model against its counterpart black-box model on two tasks: 1) classification of data from familiar classes, and 2) classification of data from previously unseen classes at the appropriate level in the taxonomy. We find that our model performs approximately as well as its counterpart black-box model while allowing for each classification to be interpreted.

papers.title: Bi-ICE: An Inner Interpretable Framework for Image Classification via Bi-directional Interactions between Concept and Input Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we design an interpretable framework for image classification that provides transparency at multiple levels (computational, algorithmic, implementation) via bi-directional interactions between concept and input embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Bi-ICE module, which enables inner interpretability for image classification by facilitating bi-directional interactions between concept and input embeddings, allowing for multilevel analysis (computational, algorithmic, implementation) and maintaining or improving model performance.
papers.conclusion: Bi-ICE provides a framework for inner interpretability in image classification, offering transparency at computational, algorithmic, and implementation levels through bi-directional interactions between concept and input embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Integrating the Bi-ICE module maintains or slightly improves the classification performance of backbone models (ViT, ResNet) while adding interpretability.
The module enables concept-based explanations, quantifying concept contributions and localizing them within input images.
Concept vectors converge to semantically meaningful clusters over training epochs, demonstrating the model's ability to learn interpretable concepts even without ground-truth annotations.
The framework supports analysis at computational (concept contributions), algorithmic (concept learning dynamics), and implementation (concept localization) levels.
Experiments on CUB-200-2011 show that Bi-ICE effectively identifies and utilizes key concepts for prediction, as validated by concept insertion and deletion evaluations.
papers.abstract: Inner interpretability is a promising field aiming to uncover the internal mechanisms of AI systems through scalable, automated methods. While significant research has been conducted on large language models, limited attention has been paid to applying inner interpretability to large-scale image tasks, focusing primarily on architectural and functional levels to visualize learned concepts. In this paper, we first present a conceptual framework that supports inner interpretability and multilevel analysis for large-scale image classification tasks. Specifically, we introduce the Bi-directional Interaction between Concept and Input Embeddings (Bi-ICE) module, which facilitates interpretability across the computational, algorithmic, and implementation levels. This module enhances transparency by generating predictions based on human-understandable concepts, quantifying their contributions, and localizing them within the inputs. Finally, we showcase enhanced transparency in image classification, measuring concept contributions, and pinpointing their locations within the inputs. Our approach highlights algorithmic interpretability by demonstrating the process of concept learning and its convergence.

papers.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Why does in-context learning (ICL) emerge and then disappear (transience) during training, and what are the dynamics between ICL and other learning strategies?
papers.core_contribution: The transience of in-context learning (ICL) is explained by coopetition (cooperative and competitive dynamics) between ICL and a newly identified strategy called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), where shared sub-circuits enable ICL emergence before CIWL asymptotically dominates.
papers.conclusion: Strategy coopetition between ICL and CIWL explains the emergence and transience of ICL, providing a deeper mechanistic understanding of how capabilities dynamically trade off during transformer training.
papers.key_findings:
The asymptotic strategy after ICL transience is a hybrid called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), which depends on both in-weights information and the presence of the correct label in context.
ICL and CIWL share critical sub-circuits (e.g., Layer 2 induction heads), leading to cooperative dynamics that enable ICL emergence.
ICL emergence is only possible when CIWL is not fully formed, and ICL is faster to emerge but asymptotically dominated by CIWL.
A minimal mathematical model captures the coopetition dynamics and explains transience.
Matching context and query exemplars in the data can make ICL persistent by removing the asymptotic bias towards CIWL.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a powerful ability that emerges in transformer models, enabling them to learn from context without weight updates. Recent work has established emergent ICL as a transient phenomenon that can sometimes disappear after long training times. In this work, we sought a mechanistic understanding of these transient dynamics. Firstly, we find that, after the disappearance of ICL, the asymptotic strategy is a remarkable hybrid between in-weights and in-context learning, which we term "context-constrained in-weights learning" (CIWL). CIWL is in competition with ICL, and eventually replaces it as the dominant strategy of the model (thus leading to ICL transience). However, we also find that the two competing strategies actually share sub-circuits, which gives rise to cooperative dynamics as well. For example, in our setup, ICL is unable to emerge quickly on its own, and can only be enabled through the simultaneous slow development of asymptotic CIWL. CIWL thus both cooperates and competes with ICL, a phenomenon we term "strategy coopetition." We propose a minimal mathematical model that reproduces these key dynamics and interactions. Informed by this model, we were able to identify a setup where ICL is truly emergent and persistent.

papers.title: Integrating clinical reasoning into large language model-based diagnosis through etiology-aware attention steering
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex clinical scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: This study proposes an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework that integrates structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis by identifying and steering attention heads crucial for etiology reasoning, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and reasoning focus.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework integrates etiology-aware attention guidance with authoritative clinical guidelines, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy, attention stability, and reasoning interpretability, holding strong potential for real-world clinical deployment in complex diagnostic environments.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines on the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort.
External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort confirms the framework's effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy in real-world complex scenarios.
The Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm successfully pinpoints attention heads that exhibit strong alignment with etiological reasoning.
Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of each component (CRS annotation, Etiology-Aware Head Identification, Reasoning-Guided Loss) for overall performance.
The framework enhances the model's attention stability and reasoning interpretability across diverse diagnostic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to a broader range of diseases and clinical scenarios.
Integrating multimodal data (e.g., medical images, lab waveforms) to enhance diagnostic reasoning.
Incorporating contrastive or self-supervised objectives to further enhance model robustness in low-resource or noisy environments.
papers.abstract: Objective: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant capabilities in medical text understanding and generation. However, their diagnostic reliability in complex clinical scenarios remains limited. This study aims to enhance LLMs' diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability. Method: We propose an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework to integrate structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis. Specifically, we first construct Clinical Reasoning Scaffolding (CRS) based on authoritative clinical guidelines for three representative acute abdominal emergencies: acute appendicitis, acute pancreatitis, and acute cholecystitis. Next, we develop the Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm to pinpoint attention heads crucial for the model's etiology reasoning. To ensure reliable clinical reasoning alignment, we introduce the Reasoning-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning that embeds etiological reasoning cues into input representations and steers the selected Etiology-Aware Heads toward critical information through a Reasoning-Guided Loss function. Result: On the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort, our framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines. External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort further confirms its effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Further assessments via Reasoning Attention Frequency indicate that our models exhibit enhanced reliability when faced with real-world complex scenarios. Conclusion: This study presents a practical and effective approach to enhance clinical reasoning in LLM-based diagnosis. By aligning model attention with structured CRS, the proposed framework offers a promising paradigm for building more interpretable and reliable AI diagnostic systems in complex clinical settings.

papers.title: Unsupervised Interpretable Basis Extraction for Concept-Based Visual Explanations
papers.research_question: How can we extract an interpretable basis for CNN intermediate layer feature spaces without requiring annotated concept datasets?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised post-hoc method to extract an interpretable basis for CNN intermediate layer feature spaces, which improves interpretability metrics and reveals that supervised approaches are limited to a single direction per concept.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an unsupervised post-hoc method for interpretable basis extraction, demonstrates its effectiveness across architectures, and compares it with supervised approaches, providing insights for future research.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed unsupervised method extracts bases that are more interpretable than the natural basis according to the proposed metrics S1 and S2.
The method can cover multiple directions for the same concept, which is a limitation of supervised approaches that learn only one direction per concept.
However, devoting multiple directions to a single concept limits the number of unique concepts that can be described by the basis.
The method is effective across different CNN architectures (ResNet18, VGG16BN, AlexNet, GoogleNet) and training datasets (Places365, ImageNet).
Intermediate layer representations become more interpretable when projected onto the bases extracted with the proposed method.
papers.limitation:
The method may assign multiple basis vectors to the same concept, limiting the number of unique concepts covered.
The method assumes orthogonality, which may not hold for positively correlated concepts.
future_direction: Consider approximately orthogonal and over-complete bases (I > D) to improve the number of unique concepts covered.
papers.abstract: An important line of research attempts to explain CNN image classifier predictions and intermediate layer representations in terms of human understandable concepts. In this work, we expand on previous works in the literature that use annotated concept datasets to extract interpretable feature space directions and propose an unsupervised post-hoc method to extract a disentangling interpretable basis by looking for the rotation of the feature space that explains sparse one-hot thresholded transformed representations of pixel activations.
