We do experimentation with existing popular CNNs and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in extracting an interpretable basis across network architectures and training datasets. We make extensions to the existing basis interpretability metrics found in the literature and show that, intermediate layer representations become more interpretable when transformed to the bases extracted with our method. Finally, using the basis interpretability metrics, we compare the bases extracted with our method with the bases derived with a supervised approach and find that, in one aspect, the proposed unsupervised approach has a strength that constitutes a limitation of the supervised one and give potential directions for future research.

papers.title: DILA: Dictionary Label Attention for Mechanistic Interpretability in High-dimensional Multi-label Medical Coding Prediction
papers.research_question: How to provide comprehensive, global explanations for high-dimensional multi-label predictions, specifically in medical coding, by disentangling dense embeddings into interpretable sparse concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DILA, a mechanistic interpretability module that uses dictionary learning to create sparse, interpretable embeddings and a sparse matrix mapping these features to labels, providing global explanations for multi-label predictions while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: DILA provides a scalable and effective approach for mechanistic interpretability in high-dimensional multi-label prediction, successfully balancing interpretability, performance, and computational efficiency for tasks like medical coding.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse dictionary features from DILA are at least 50% more human-interpretable than dense embeddings.
An automated pipeline using medical LLMs can identify and summarize thousands of learned medical concepts from the sparse features.
DILA maintains competitive performance with state-of-the-art black-box models on the MIMIC-III clean medical coding dataset.
Ablating weights in the global sparse projection matrix (Aficd) precisely affects only the target ICD code prediction, unlike token-level perturbations which affect multiple codes.
Mechanistic interpretability via DILA is computationally efficient compared to model-agnostic methods like KernelSHAP for high-dimensional tasks.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary features are not always perfectly interpretable, and the LLM-based auto-interpretability pipeline can be improved.
DILA's performance is slightly lower than some black-box baselines.
future_direction: Improving the auto-interpretability pipeline with better LLM prompting and feature identification.
Extending the method to other domains and tasks beyond medical coding.
papers.abstract: Predicting high-dimensional or extreme multilabels, such as in medical coding, requires both accuracy and interpretability. Existing works often rely on local interpretability methods, failing to provide comprehensive explanations of the overall mechanism behind each label prediction within a multilabel set. We propose a mechanistic interpretability module called DIctionary Label Attention (\method) that disentangles uninterpretable dense embeddings into a sparse embedding space, where each nonzero element (a dictionary feature) represents a globally learned medical concept. Through human evaluations, we show that our sparse embeddings are more human understandable than its dense counterparts by at least 50 percent. Our automated dictionary feature identification pipeline, leveraging large language models (LLMs), uncovers thousands of learned medical concepts by examining and summarizing the highest activating tokens for each dictionary feature. We represent the relationships between dictionary features and medical codes through a sparse interpretable matrix, enhancing the mechanistic and global understanding of the model's predictions while maintaining competitive performance and scalability without extensive human annotation.

papers.title: Is attention required for ICL? Exploring the Relationship Between Model Architecture and In-Context Learning Ability
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between model architecture and in-context learning ability? Which architectures are capable of ICL and which exhibit superior performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that in-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with some attention alternatives being competitive with or better than transformers in certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with attention alternatives being competitive. However, no architecture is consistent across all tasks, and performance degrades with out-of-distribution prompt lengths.
papers.key_findings:
All considered architectures can perform in-context learning, demonstrating ICL is not exclusive to attention-based models.
Attention alternatives such as Mamba, Hyena, RetNet, and RWKV are sometimes competitive with or better than transformers at ICL.
Performance varies with number of in-context examples; some architectures show degradation when extrapolating to longer prompts than seen in training.
The emergence of ICL in image classification is influenced by burstiness in training data; some architectures are predisposed towards memorization over ICL.
ICL score in language modeling correlates with performance on other ICL tasks, but not perfectly.
papers.abstract: What is the relationship between model architecture and the ability to perform in-context learning? In this empirical study, we take the first steps toward answering this question. We evaluate thirteen model architectures capable of causal language modeling across a suite of synthetic in-context learning tasks. These selected architectures represent a broad range of paradigms, including recurrent and convolution-based neural networks, transformers, state space model inspired, and other emerging attention alternatives. We discover that all the considered architectures can perform in-context learning under a wider range of conditions than previously documented. Additionally, we observe stark differences in statistical efficiency and consistency by varying the number of in-context examples and task difficulty. We also measure each architecture's predisposition towards in-context learning when presented with the option to memorize rather than leverage in-context examples. Finally, and somewhat surprisingly, we find that several attention alternatives are sometimes competitive with or better in-context learners than transformers. However, no single architecture demonstrates consistency across all tasks, with performance either plateauing or declining when confronted with a significantly larger number of in-context examples than those encountered during gradient-based training.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What are the precise training dynamics during the emergence of induction heads for in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a simple, interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing induction heads and proves that training dynamics are constrained to a low-dimensional subspace, with only three parameters accounting for the emergence.
papers.conclusion: This work shows how induction heads emerge in an ICL task and paves the way for a better theoretical understanding of transformer learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrices of an induction head have a simple structure described by three pseudo-parameters (α3, β2, γ3).
Training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace, and only three dimensions are necessary for the induction head to emerge.
The emergence time of the induction head is quadratic in the context length (Θ(N^2)).
The three parameters emerge in a specific order: γ first, then β, then α.
The emergence of the induction head is self-contained, unaided by the other parameters.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope is limited to a disentangled, attention-only transformer; production models with LayerNorm, MLPs, and additive residual streams may have different dynamics.
Theoretical results assume orthonormal inputs and zero initialization, which may not hold in practice and could alter emergence times.
The study uses a simplified ICL task (exact matching of item-label pairs), not natural language with its complexities.
future_direction: Exploring how data distributional properties like burstiness modulate the effective context length and emergence.
Investigating other means of reducing effective context length, such as special positional embeddings.
Applying a similar approach to study other phenomena like the in-context vs. in-weights learning trade-off, abrupt learning, or other transformer circuits.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant architecture for natural language processing. Part of their success is owed to a remarkable capability known as in-context learning (ICL): they can acquire and apply novel associations solely from their input context, without any updates to their weights. In this work, we study the emergence of induction heads, a previously identified mechanism in two-layer transformers that is particularly important for in-context learning. We uncover a relatively simple and interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing the induction head. We theoretically explain the origin of this structure using a minimal ICL task formulation and a modified transformer architecture. We give a formal proof that the training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace of the parameter space. Empirically, we validate this constraint while observing that only 3 dimensions account for the emergence of an induction head. By further studying the training dynamics inside this 3-dimensional subspace, we find that the time until the emergence of an induction head follows a tight asymptotic bound that is quadratic in the input context length.

papers.title: To Sink or Not to Sink: Visual Information Pathways in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental benefits of ViT attention sink tokens in large vision-language models, and how can they be understood and operationalized to improve visual reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes ViT attention sinks in LVLMs, finding they encode high-level semantic context, and introduces DIYSink, a framework that dynamically leverages these sinks to improve visual reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: ViT attention sinks are important carriers of high-level visual context and can be effectively leveraged, both via training-free and training-based methods, to enhance the visual reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models.
papers.key_findings:
ViT sink tokens propagate into the LLM, activating distinct hidden dimensions different from LLM-emerged sinks.
ViT sinks capture coarse-grained, high-level contextual features and are semantically meaningful.
ViT sinks are beneficial for global tasks requiring high-level understanding but can degrade performance on local, detail-rich tasks.
A simple training-free approach (sink-to-the-front) improves performance across various LVLMs.
The proposed DIYSink framework, with dual MLP projectors and dynamic token selection, yields substantial improvements across a range of benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The proposed DIYSink framework requires access to training data and computational resources for training from scratch.
future_direction: Extending DIYSink to other modalities such as video and audio.
papers.abstract: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) have recently emerged as powerful architectures capable of understanding and reasoning over both visual and textual information. These models typically rely on two key components: a Vision Transformer (ViT) and a Large Language Model (LLM). ViT encodes visual content into a sequence of image tokens and serves as the perceptual front-end -- the eyes of the model. In contrast, the LLM interprets these tokens to perform high-level reasoning, generates responses, and functions as the cognitive core -- the brain of the model. However, it remains unclear which visual tokens contribute most significantly to understanding and reasoning, and how effectively these signals are propagated from ViT to the LLM. While most existing works have focused on identifying attention sinks, low-semantic tokens receiving disproportionately high attention, within the LLM, we shift the focus to the vision encoder by identifying a class of high-norm visual tokens from ViT, referred to as ViT attention sinks -- a problem that has been rarely studied but is indeed very important for LVLMs. Our findings show that these ViT sinks encapsulate high-level semantic concepts from images, allowing the LLM to perform more effective understanding and reasoning. Despite their importance, these sink tokens are often overlooked in existing LVLM architectures. To explore their contribution, we present both qualitative and quantitative analyses of the information embedded in these sink tokens. We also propose both training-free and training-based approaches to better leverage how this information is interpreted by the LLM, and to what extent. By explicitly utilizing these tokens, we demonstrate substantial improvements across a range of LVLMs and visual reasoning tasks, highlighting the untapped potential of ViT attention sinks in enhancing visual reasoning.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: A Multimodal and Interpretable Deep Learning Framework for Early Detection of Blood Cancer Using Clinical Data
papers.research_question: How can a multimodal deep learning framework integrate patient symptoms, imaging, and laboratory results to provide accurate and interpretable early detection of blood cancer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a multimodal and interpretable deep learning framework (MIDLF) that integrates patient symptoms, medical imaging, and laboratory results using a gated attention mechanism and explainability tools (SHAP, LRP) to achieve high-accuracy, early detection of blood cancer.
papers.conclusion: The proposed multimodal and interpretable framework effectively integrates diverse clinical data for early blood cancer detection, providing accurate and explainable predictions, though its generalizability is limited by reliance on a single dataset.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed MIDLF framework achieved an accuracy of 94.8% and an AUC-ROC of 97.1% on the BIOBANK dataset, outperforming baseline models CSNN and TSFS-TCEM.
The framework's interpretability outputs, generated via SHAP and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, were validated by clinicians and highlighted clinically relevant features such as persistent fatigue, elevated WBC count, and abnormal blood clusters.
The gated attention mechanism effectively fused multimodal data (symptoms, imaging, lab results), capturing relationships across modalities for improved prediction.
The framework demonstrated robust performance across different blood cancer subtypes, maintaining over 90% accuracy for each.
Preprocessing techniques, including graph-based symptom embedding, self-supervised image preprocessing, and GAN-based missing data imputation, were crucial for handling heterogeneous clinical data.
papers.limitation: Reliance on data from a single dataset (BIOBANK), which may limit generalizability across diverse populations.
future_direction: Incorporating more diverse datasets to improve generalizability.
Exploring the framework's application to additional medical conditions.
Enhancing the interpretability module to improve usability in clinical settings.
papers.abstract: Diagnosing blood cancer at early stages presents challenges due to limitations in methods that rely on single data sources, which often fail to provide comprehensive insights. The study introduces a Multimodal and Interpretable Deep Learning Framework (MIDLF) that combines patient symptoms, imaging, and laboratory results to predict blood cancer with explainable outputs. The framework integrates a graph-based model for encoding symptoms, a hybrid Vision Transformer (ViT) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for imaging analysis, and an attention-driven module for laboratory data. A gated attention mechanism fuses these inputs, capturing relationships across modalities. Preprocessing includes graph-based embeddings for symptoms, self-supervised learning for unlabeled imaging data, and generative models to address missing laboratory values. Evaluation used the BIOBANK dataset, which includes multimodal clinical data. The framework achieved an accuracy of 94.8%, a recall of 95.2%, and an AUC-ROC of 97.1%. These results were benchmarked against Cell Scoring Neural Network (CSNN) and Three-Stage Feature Selection with Twice-Competitional Ensemble Learning Method (TSFS-TCEM), demonstrating improved prediction consistency across metrics. Clinician reviews validated feature importance outputs from SHAP and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, showing alignment with clinical reasoning. This framework addresses challenges in integrating diverse clinical data and explaining model predictions. Results suggest that combining symptoms, imaging, and laboratory data enables more informed diagnostic predictions, facilitating early detection of blood cancer.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Probing and Boosting Large Language Models Capabilities via Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How can we establish a correspondence between fundamental LLM capabilities and internal attention heads, and leverage this correspondence for targeted instruction tuning to improve model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a correspondence between fundamental LLM capabilities and internal attention heads, and leverages this correspondence for targeted instruction tuning via a lightweight, gradient-free data selection method.
papers.conclusion: The paper systematically explored the correspondence between fundamental application capabilities and attention mechanisms, revealing capability-attention head correspondence, practical effectiveness, and capability composability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can be used to predict specific capabilities with over 70% discrimination accuracy.
The top-16 attention heads for different capabilities show little overlap, indicating high discriminability of the capability taxonomy.
Using capability-specific attention heads for data selection improves performance on MMLU and BBH, outperforming gradient-based (LESS) and other intermediate-state baselines.
Performance improves with up to 16 concatenated attention heads but degrades with 32 heads due to increased overlap and reduced discriminability.
A certain volume of high-quality data (4-5%) is sufficient for capability enhancement; adding more mixed data can be detrimental.
papers.limitation: Experimental validation is limited to models up to 8B parameters due to computational resource constraints.
future_direction: Leverage activation patterns of capability-specific attention heads to provide interpretability for LLM outputs.
Restrict fine-tuning to only capability-specific heads for more fine-grained model adaptation.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Analyzing Hierarchical Structure in Vision Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Do the internal representations of vision models align with the ImageNet hierarchy, and can Sparse Autoencoders reveal this structure? How consistent is this structure across different layers, and can SAE-derived representations quantify the degree to which a model respects taxonomic relationships?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Autoencoders as a tool for analyzing hierarchical structure in vision models, demonstrating that SAEs can reveal how DINOv2 encodes ImageNet taxonomic relationships in its representations, with increasing information in later layers.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are effective for probing hierarchical structure in vision models, revealing that DINOv2 implicitly encodes taxonomic information, with stronger alignment in later layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers of DINOv2's class token contain little information, while later layers gain more hierarchical information.
SAEs extract features that align with ImageNet hierarchy, with higher ontological coverage in later layers.
Specific SAE heads capture higher-order concepts such as elasmodranch, whales, woodwind instruments, and warships.
SAE metrics can serve as a surrogate for identifying information in representations without the need for labels.
The model encodes hierarchical concepts increasingly through each processing layer.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a single vision foundation model, DINOv2, and may not generalize to all architectures.
Focus on ImageNet hierarchy, which may not be comprehensive or universally applicable for all visual concepts.
Reliance on SAEs introduces interpretability challenges, such as feature redundancy or artifacts from sparsity constraints.
Hierarchical metrics may not fully capture all nuances of taxonomic representation within vision models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to diverse models and taxonomies, including those from human perception studies.
Use advanced XAI methods, such as causal interventions, to further clarify hierarchical encoding.
Apply SAEs to hierarchical classification and concept-based model editing.
papers.abstract: The ImageNet hierarchy provides a structured taxonomy of object categories, offering a valuable lens through which to analyze the representations learned by deep vision models. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of how vision models encode the ImageNet hierarchy, leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to probe their internal representations. SAEs have been widely used as an explanation tool for large language models (LLMs), where they enable the discovery of semantically meaningful features. Here, we extend their use to vision models to investigate whether learned representations align with the ontological structure defined by the ImageNet taxonomy. Our results show that SAEs uncover hierarchical relationships in model activations, revealing an implicit encoding of taxonomic structure. We analyze the consistency of these representations across different layers of the popular vision foundation model DINOv2 and provide insights into how deep vision models internalize hierarchical category information by increasing information in the class token through each layer. Our study establishes a framework for systematic hierarchical analysis of vision model representations and highlights the potential of SAEs as a tool for probing semantic structure in deep networks.

papers.title: A Weakly Supervised Gradient Attribution Constraint for Interpretable Classification and Anomaly Detection
papers.research_question: How can we constrain a deep classification network during training so that its decision is based on relevant pathological structures, thereby improving interpretability and enabling weakly supervised anomaly detection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new weakly supervised loss function that constrains gradient-based attributions during classifier training, forcing healthy image regions to drive the decision towards the healthy class, which improves interpretability and enables unsupervised pathology segmentation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed weakly supervised gradient attribution constraint makes classifier decisions more interpretable and pathology-driven, while also providing state-of-the-art performance for anomaly detection, with the practical advantage that constraining with Gradient attributions is sufficient and more efficient than using Expected Gradients.
papers.key_findings:
Constraining training with simple Gradient (G) attributions is computationally cheaper and yields results equivalent to using Expected Gradient (EG) constraints.
The proposed attribution constraint leads to more pathology-focused decisions and improves both classification interpretability and anomaly detection performance.
The method outperforms state-of-the-art interpretable classification and anomaly detection methods on brain tumor and multiple sclerosis tasks.
A combined attribution constraint (IEG) during training makes the model robust to the choice of gradient-based attribution method used at inference.
future_direction: Extend the method to other deep models like GANs for anomaly detection.
Apply the constraint to other tasks such as regression, disease grade estimation, and image registration.
papers.abstract: The lack of interpretability of deep learning reduces understanding of what happens when a network does not work as expected and hinders its use in critical fields like medicine, which require transparency of decisions. For example, a healthy vs pathological classification model should rely on radiological signs and not on some training dataset biases. Several post-hoc models have been proposed to explain the decision of a trained network. However, they are very seldom used to enforce interpretability during training and none in accordance with the classification. In this paper, we propose a new weakly supervised method for both interpretable healthy vs pathological classification and anomaly detection. A new loss function is added to a standard classification model to constrain each voxel of healthy images to drive the network decision towards the healthy class according to gradient-based attributions. This constraint reveals pathological structures for patient images, allowing their unsupervised segmentation. Moreover, we advocate both theoretically and experimentally, that constrained training with the simple Gradient attribution is similar to constraints with the heavier Expected Gradient, consequently reducing the computational cost. We also propose a combination of attributions during the constrained training making the model robust to the attribution choice at inference. Our proposition was evaluated on two brain pathologies: tumors and multiple sclerosis. This new constraint provides a more relevant classification, with a more pathology-driven decision. For anomaly detection, the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art especially on difficult multiple sclerosis lesions segmentation task with a 15 points Dice improvement.

papers.title: A Test Statistic Estimation-Based Approach for Establishing Self-Interpretable CNN-Based Binary Classifiers
papers.research_question: How can a self-interpretable model be established for a pre-trained deep binary black-box medical image classifier while maintaining similar classification accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: A novel decision-theory-inspired approach to establish a self-interpretable binary classifier using an encoder-decoder network that produces an equivalency map, maintaining accuracy comparable to a black-box classifier while providing quantitative visual interpretations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully establishes self-interpretable classifiers that match the performance of black-box models and provide stable, quantitative interpretations via equivalency maps for medical image classification.
papers.key_findings:
The self-interpretable network achieved classification accuracy similar to the original black-box classifier across three medical image tasks.
The equivalency maps (E-maps) highlight regions corresponding to abnormalities in medical images, providing visual interpretability.
The E-maps are stable across different random weight initializations, as measured by high SSIM scores.
Quantitative analysis shows high overlap between top-contributing E-map pixels and annotated abnormality regions.
The method avoids trivial zero-padded solutions under typical random weight initializations.
papers.limitation:
The method is currently designed for binary classification tasks; extension to multi-class problems is suggested but not implemented.
There exists a potential trivial zero-padded solution, but it is unlikely to occur with standard random weight initialization.
future_direction: Extend the proposed approach to multi-class classification problems.
Apply the method to other domains beyond medical imaging.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is highly desired for deep neural network-based classifiers, especially when addressing high-stake decisions in medical imaging. Commonly used post-hoc interpretability methods have the limitation that they can produce plausible but different interpretations of a given model, leading to ambiguity about which one to choose. To address this problem, a novel decision-theory-inspired approach is investigated to establish a self-interpretable model, given a pre-trained deep binary black-box medical image classifier. This approach involves utilizing a self-interpretable encoder-decoder model in conjunction with a single-layer fully connected network with unity weights. The model is trained to estimate the test statistic of the given trained black-box deep binary classifier to maintain a similar accuracy. The decoder output image, referred to as an equivalency map, is an image that represents a transformed version of the to-be-classified image that, when processed by the fixed fully connected layer, produces the same test statistic value as the original classifier. The equivalency map provides a visualization of the transformed image features that directly contribute to the test statistic value and, moreover, permits quantification of their relative contributions. Unlike the traditional post-hoc interpretability methods, the proposed method is self-interpretable, quantitative. Detailed quantitative and qualitative analyses have been performed with three different medical image binary classification tasks.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Deep Supervised, but Not Unsupervised, Models May Explain IT Cortical Representation
papers.research_question: To what extent can the internal representations of computational object-vision models explain the representational geometry of primate inferior temporal (IT) cortex?
papers.core_contribution: Supervised deep learning models, particularly a deep convolutional network trained on ImageNet, best explain the representational geometry of primate IT cortex, and combining their features with linear discriminants can fully explain the IT data, whereas unsupervised models fail to account for the categorical clustering in IT.
papers.conclusion: Explaining IT cortical representation requires computational features trained through supervised learning with large labeled datasets to emphasize behaviorally important categorical divisions.
papers.key_findings:
Better performing models in object categorization show higher representational similarity to IT cortex.
Unsupervised models fail to explain the categorical clustering (e.g., animate/inanimate, face clusters) observed in IT.
A deep supervised convolutional network (trained on ImageNet) best explains IT representation but does not fully explain it.
Combining features from the deep supervised model with linear discriminants (trained to maximize categorical margins) yields a representation that fully explains the IT data.
Model representations that are more similar to IT also afford better categorization accuracy.
papers.abstract: Inferior temporal (IT) cortex in human and nonhuman primates serves visual object recognition. Computational object-vision models, although continually improving, do not yet reach human performance. It is unclear to what extent the internal representations of computational models can explain the IT representation. Here we investigate a wide range of computational model representations (37 in total), testing their categorization performance and their ability to account for the IT representational geometry. The models include well-known neuroscientific object-recognition models (e.g. HMAX, VisNet) along with several models from computer vision (e.g. SIFT, GIST, self-similarity features, and a deep convolutional neural network). We compared the representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) of the model representations with the RDMs obtained from human IT (measured with fMRI) and monkey IT (measured with cell recording) for the same set of stimuli (not used in training the models). Better performing models were more similar to IT in that they showed greater clustering of representational patterns by category. In addition, better performing models also more strongly resembled IT in terms of their within-category representational dissimilarities. Representational geometries were significantly correlated between IT and many of the models. However, the categorical clustering observed in IT was largely unexplained by the unsupervised models. The deep convolutional network, which was trained by supervision with over a million category-labeled images, reached the highest categorization performance and also best explained IT, although it did not fully explain the IT data. Combining the features of this model with appropriate weights and adding linear combinations that maximize the margin between animate and inanimate objects and between faces and other objects yielded a representation that fully explained our IT data. Overall, our results suggest that explaining IT requires computational features trained through supervised learning to emphasize the behaviorally important categorical divisions prominently reflected in IT.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Fine-Tuned Vision Transformers on Distorted Images: Decoding Attention Head Behavior for Transparent and Trustworthy AI
papers.research_question: How do individual attention heads in vision transformers process relevant versus extraneous information when fine-tuned on distorted images containing non-relevant content?
papers.core_contribution: This study uses attention map extraction and ablation analysis to show functional specialization in fine-tuned Vision Transformers, identifying monosemantic heads that focus on task-relevant features (chirp localization) and non-task-relevant features (text, edges), as well as polysemantic heads that attend to multiple irrelevant regions.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability, through attention map analysis and ablation, reveals functional specialization in Vision Transformers, enhancing model understanding and identifying components critical for task performance versus those processing irrelevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating attention heads in early layers (1-3) results in minimal performance impact, suggesting they focus on less critical low-level features.
Ablating deeper heads (e.g., in layer 6) causes a threefold higher loss increase, indicating greater importance for the regression task.
Intermediate layers (6-11) contain monosemantic heads that attend exclusively to the chirp region in spectrograms.
Some early heads (1-4) are monosemantic but non-task-relevant, specializing in detecting features like text, color bars, and edges/corners.
Attention maps can distinguish monosemantic heads (precise localization) from polysemantic heads (attending to multiple irrelevant regions).
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability improves the safety, reliability, and robustness of large AI models. This study examined individual attention heads in vision transformers (ViTs) fine tuned on distorted 2D spectrogram images containing non relevant content (axis labels, titles, color bars). By introducing extraneous features, the study analyzed how transformer components processed unrelated information, using mechanistic interpretability to debug issues and reveal insights into transformer architectures. Attention maps assessed head contributions across layers. Heads in early layers (1 to 3) showed minimal task impact with ablation increased MSE loss slightly ({\mu}=0.11%, {\sigma}=0.09%), indicating focus on less critical low level features. In contrast, deeper heads (e.g., layer 6) caused a threefold higher loss increase ({\mu}=0.34%, {\sigma}=0.02%), demonstrating greater task importance. Intermediate layers (6 to 11) exhibited monosemantic behavior, attending exclusively to chirp regions. Some early heads (1 to 4) were monosemantic but non task relevant (e.g. text detectors, edge or corner detectors). Attention maps distinguished monosemantic heads (precise chirp localization) from polysemantic heads (multiple irrelevant regions). These findings revealed functional specialization in ViTs, showing how heads processed relevant vs. extraneous information. By decomposing transformers into interpretable components, this work enhanced model understanding, identified vulnerabilities, and advanced safer, more transparent AI.

papers.title: Interpretable AI for bio-medical applications
papers.research_question: How can LIME and SHAP be used to explain the predictions of a deep neural network trained on the UCI Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset, and what insights do they provide?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how LIME and SHAP can be used to explain predictions of a deep neural network on the UCI Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset, providing insights into feature contributions that align with medical expertise.
papers.conclusion: LIME and SHAP are valuable tools for explaining DNN predictions in biomedical applications, helping to build trust in AI systems by providing interpretable insights.
papers.key_findings:
LIME and SHAP provide consistent explanations for the DNN's predictions, with higher feature values indicating malignancy and lower values indicating benign masses, which aligns with medical understanding.
SHAP provides a holistic view of feature importance across the dataset, while LIME explains individual predictions.
The DNN achieved 97% accuracy on the test set.
The most important features for classification are the 'worst' values of radius, texture, and concave points.
SHAP dependency plots reveal linear relationships between some features and their Shapley values, and interactions between features.
papers.limitation: LIME and SHAP require running the trained model multiple times, which may not be suitable for real-time explanations, especially for larger neural networks.
future_direction: Using LIME and SHAP for datasets with more than two output classes.
Using abstract features derived within the DNN as input to LIME and SHAP to understand their relevance and for transfer learning.
papers.abstract: This paper presents the use of two popular explainability tools called Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to explain the predictions made by a trained deep neural network. The deep neural network used in this work is trained on the UCI Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset. The neural network is used to classify the masses found in patients as benign or malignant based on 30 features that describe the mass. LIME and SHAP are then used to explain the individual predictions made by the trained neural network model. The explanations provide further insights into the relationship between the input features and the predictions. SHAP methodology additionally provides a more holistic view of the effect of the inputs on the output predictions. The results also present the commonalities between the insights gained using LIME and SHAP. Although this paper focuses on the use of deep neural networks trained on UCI Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset, the methodology can be applied to other neural networks and architectures trained on other applications. The deep neural network trained in this work provides a high level of accuracy. Analyzing the model using LIME and SHAP adds the much desired benefit of providing explanations for the recommendations made by the trained model.

papers.title: Beyond Scalars: Concept-Based Alignment Analysis in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: How can concept discovery be combined with alignment analysis to provide fine-grained insights into the structures within and differences between latent activations in Vision Transformers, beyond scalar alignment measures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a concept-based alignment analysis method that combines nonlinear manifold concept discovery (NLMCD) with a generalized Rand index to enable fine-grained comparison of representations in Vision Transformers, revealing universal and unique concepts.
papers.conclusion: Concept-based alignment analysis provides detailed insights into the structuredness of latent spaces in ViTs, guiding model selection and understanding of representation differences beyond scalar alignment measures.
papers.key_findings:
Increased supervision in training correlates with a reduction in the semantic structure of learned representations in ViTs.
The fully supervised (FS) model exhibits a nucleation process where concepts form abruptly in later layers, unlike self-supervised models.
Self-supervised models (CLIP, DINO, MAE) show smoother concept formation and higher semantic organization in their representations.
Concept-based alignment reveals that basic foundational features are learned similarly across models in early layers, while later layers diverge based on pre-training tasks.
The proposed NLMCD method outperforms linear concept definitions for alignment analysis in a sanity check.
papers.limitation:
Computational scalability of HDBSCAN limits the sampling of feature vectors, causing under-sampled concept regions to appear as noise.
The limited variability of ImageNet-1k might obfuscate concept meanings, e.g., when a concept represents a color but only specific object patches of that color are present.
papers.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) can be trained using various learning paradigms, from fully supervised to self-supervised. Diverse training protocols often result in significantly different feature spaces, which are usually compared through alignment analysis. However, current alignment measures quantify this relationship in terms of a single scalar value, obscuring the distinctions between common and unique features in pairs of representations that share the same scalar alignment. We address this limitation by combining alignment analysis with concept discovery, which enables a breakdown of alignment into single concepts encoded in feature space. This fine-grained comparison reveals both universal and unique concepts across different representations, as well as the internal structure of concepts within each of them. Our methodological contributions address two key prerequisites for concept-based alignment: 1) For a description of the representation in terms of concepts that faithfully capture the geometry of the feature space, we define concepts as the most general structure they can possibly form - arbitrary manifolds, allowing hidden features to be described by their proximity to these manifolds. 2) To measure distances between concept proximity scores of two representations, we use a generalized Rand index and partition it for alignment between pairs of concepts. We confirm the superiority of our novel concept definition for alignment analysis over existing linear baselines in a sanity check. The concept-based alignment analysis of representations from four different ViTs reveals that increased supervision correlates with a reduction in the semantic structure of learned representations.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Visual Concept Connectome (VCC): Open World Concept Discovery and their Interlayer Connections in Deep Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover human-interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections in deep vision models in a fully unsupervised manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Visual Concept Connectome (VCC), a method for unsupervised discovery of human-interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections in deep vision models, enabling holistic analysis of network structure and application to tasks like failure debugging.
papers.conclusion: VCCs provide a method for unsupervised discovery of interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections, revealing interesting properties of deep models and enabling applications like failure debugging.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers have more but weaker concepts, while later layers have fewer but stronger concepts.
CNNs and transformers compose concepts differently, with transformers showing more diverse connection strengths in the final layer.
VCCs can be used for debugging model failures by tracing hierarchical concept contributions.
Robust and self-supervised models have fewer low-level concepts and less compositionality than standard models.
The branching factor and number of concepts vary across layers and architectures, converging to about two concepts in the final layer.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Silhouette method for selecting the number of clusters during segmentation, which could yield different results with other methods.
Lack of a method for automatic selection of layers to analyze, which could reveal more focused patterns.
papers.abstract: Understanding what deep network models capture in their learned representations is a fundamental challenge in computer vision. We present a new methodology to understanding such vision models, the Visual Concept Connectome (VCC), which discovers human interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections in a fully unsupervised manner. Our approach simultaneously reveals fine-grained concepts at a layer, connection weightings across all layers and is amendable to global analysis of network structure (e.g., branching pattern of hierarchical concept assemblies). Previous work yielded ways to extract interpretable concepts from single layers and examine their impact on classification, but did not afford multilayer concept analysis across an entire network architecture. Quantitative and qualitative empirical results show the effectiveness of VCCs in the domain of image classification. Also, we leverage VCCs for the application of failure mode debugging to reveal where mistakes arise in deep networks.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Mechanistic Fine-tuning for In-context Learning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently fine-tune language models for in-context learning by directly controlling the attention scores of induction heads, instead of using end-to-end fine-tuning with massive data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), an efficient fine-tuning method for in-context learning that directly optimizes attention scores of induction heads, and shows that this objective is implicit in end-to-end fine-tuning, suggesting a path toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.conclusion: ABFT effectively improves ICL performance by targeting induction heads, and the work demonstrates the potential of controlling model behavior through mechanistic interpretability, opening up the future application of mechanistic controllability.
papers.key_findings:
ABFT significantly improves ICL performance with high efficiency, using only around 0.01% of the data compared to previous methods.
ABFT improves prediction consistency against prompt template and demonstration sampling variations, and reduces bias towards seen labels in unseen-label scenarios.
ABFT is more efficient in time and memory and causes less harm to out-of-domain performance compared to end-to-end fine-tuning.
The ABFT objective is implicitly contained in the end-to-end training objective on ICL-style data, suggesting that such data naturally evokes induction heads.
ABFT demonstrates the possibility of controlling model behavior through intermediate features (attention scores) without supervising the final output, a step toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.limitation:
The induction head-based explanation and ABFT apply only to classification tasks with a finite label set; extending to open-ended tasks remains an open challenge.
The control methods based on gradients and moderate amounts of data are still coarse; future work could focus on gradient-free and data-free model editing.
future_direction: Extending the method to open-ended tasks.
Developing gradient-free and data-free model editing for better mechanistic controllability.
Further improving efficiency by restricting gradient updates to specific transformer layers and automatically optimizing hyperparameters and the induction head filter.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) utilizes structured demonstration-query inputs to induce few-shot learning on Language Models (LMs), which are not originally pre-trained on ICL-style data. To bridge the gap between ICL and pre-training, some approaches fine-tune LMs on large ICL-style datasets by an end-to-end paradigm with massive computational costs. To reduce such costs, in this paper, we propose Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), utilizing the previous findings on the inner mechanism of ICL, building training objectives on the attention scores instead of the final outputs, to force the attention scores to focus on the correct label tokens presented in the context and mitigate attention scores from the wrong label tokens. Our experiments on 9 modern LMs and 8 datasets empirically find that ABFT outperforms in performance, robustness, unbiasedness, and efficiency, with only around 0.01% data cost compared to the previous methods. Moreover, our subsequent analysis finds that the end-to-end training objective contains the ABFT objective, suggesting the implicit bias of ICL-style data to the emergence of induction heads. Our work demonstrates the possibility of controlling specific module sequences within LMs to improve their behavior, opening up the future application of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Concept Visualization: Explaining the CLIP Multi-modal Embedding Using WordNet
papers.research_question: How can we explain the CLIP multi-modal embedding in a task-agnostic way, providing saliency maps for any semantic concept, including those not in the model's training set?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Concept Visualization (ConVis), a novel saliency methodology that uses lexical information from WordNet to explain the CLIP image embedding, generating task-agnostic saliency maps for any semantic concept.
papers.conclusion: Concept Visualization (ConVis) is an effective saliency methodology that exploits WordNet to explain CLIP embeddings, providing task-agnostic explanations and enabling users to gain insight into the model's perception of images.
papers.key_findings:
ConVis performs well on Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection, outperforming baselines like Maximum Logit Score and Isolation Forest.
ConVis achieves comparable performance to other saliency methods on the Weakly Supervised Object Localization (WSOL) benchmark.
A user study demonstrates that users can guess image captions from ConVis saliency maps significantly better than random chance, indicating the method provides insight into CLIP's perception.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty in recognizing small objects or objects with low contrast.
Patches from central regions of large objects may lack context for accurate recognition.
Only specific portions of an object may be considered similar to a concept (e.g., for 'person', the model often identifies greater similarity with clothing).
future_direction: Explore the use of WordNet elements other than synset definitions, as well as different knowledge graphs.
Apply ConVis to other Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) frameworks such as BLIP.
Explore Saliency Maps for more abstract concepts beyond physical objects.
Investigate using custom-shaped regions (e.g., via Segment Anything Network) instead of square patches to improve explanation quality.
papers.abstract: Advances in multi-modal embeddings, and in particular CLIP, have recently driven several breakthroughs in Computer Vision (CV). CLIP has shown impressive performance on a variety of tasks, yet, its inherently opaque architecture may hinder the application of models employing CLIP as backbone, especially in fields where trust and model explainability are imperative, such as in the medical domain. Current explanation methodologies for CV models rely on Saliency Maps computed through gradient analysis or input perturbation. However, these Saliency Maps can only be computed to explain classes relevant to the end task, often smaller in scope than the backbone training classes. In the context of models implementing CLIP as their vision backbone, a substantial portion of the information embedded within the learned representations is thus left unexplained. In this work, we propose Concept Visualization (ConVis), a novel saliency methodology that explains the CLIP embedding of an image by exploiting the multi-modal nature of the embeddings. ConVis makes use of lexical information from WordNet to compute task-agnostic Saliency Maps for any concept, not limited to concepts the end model was trained on. We validate our use of WordNet via an out of distribution detection experiment, and test ConVis on an object localization benchmark, showing that Concept Visualizations correctly identify and localize the image's semantic content. Additionally, we perform a user study demonstrating that our methodology can give users insight on the model's functioning.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Breaking the Pre-Sampling Barrier: Activation-Informed Difficulty-Aware Self-Consistency
